Introduction

[
1
]

The petitioner, TLC The Land Conservancy of
British Columbia Inc. No. S36826 (“TLC”), is a society which operates as a
land trust. Its mandate is a laudable one: firstly, to secure at-risk
environmentally sensitive properties themselves or to transfer those properties
to other parties who will hold them; and secondly, to secure conservation
covenants on other properties, all for the benefit of society and for
generations to come.

[
2
]

Unfortunately, TLC’s ambitions have outpaced its
ability to fund the fulfillment of those ambitions, both in the short and long
term. To put it bluntly, TLC does not have the financial resources to maintain
and administer the various property interests that it has secured. As such, TLC
sought and obtained creditor protection in October 2013 pursuant to the
Companies’
Creditors Arrangement Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-36 (the “
CCAA
”).

[
3
]

One of the properties which TLC holds is a
historically and culturally significant residence in West Vancouver, known as the
Binning House. TLC has received an offer to purchase that property and it now
seeks court approval of that sale to address its urgent financing needs. To some
extent, TLC’s fate in these proceedings and its ability to continue with its
restructuring efforts depends on its ability to sell the Binning House and use
the proceeds towards that end.

[
4
]

What stands in the way are various issues raised
by other persons: namely, that TLC did not properly obtain title to the Binning
House and that TLC is not entitled to either the property or its proceeds; and that
if TLC did properly obtain title, TLC is restricted from selling full title to the
Binning House by reason of certain provincial legislation, being the
Charitable
Purposes Preservation Act
, S.B.C. 2004, c. 59 (the “
CPPA
”), or common
law trust obligations.

[
5
]

The stakeholders say that this decision may
potentially have implications for other properties held by TLC. Even if that is
so (and I make no comment on that), the more specific issue here is the fate of
the Binning House. Binning House is not a revenue generating property and like many
older homes, requires substantial maintenance and repairs. Someone will have to
expend substantial sums of money for its upkeep.

[
6
]

All the stakeholders, including TLC, have
expressed an interest in ensuring that the Binning House is preserved into the
future. The sad fact though is that TLC is no longer financially able or
willing to do so. More importantly, up to this point in time, no person,
government (provincial or municipal), educational institution or charity has
come forward to take on such an undertaking, other than the purchaser now
proposed by TLC.

TLC’s Background

[
7
]

In 1996, TLC was registered as a society
pursuant to the
Society Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 433. Its stated goal
was to act as a land trust in order to protect certain lands with ecological,
agricultural or cultural importance.

[
8
]

Article 2 of TLC’s Constitution sets out its
purposes:

(a)        to
contribute to and improve the education, health and welfare of the general
public and to benefit the community as a whole by the promotion and
encouragement of the protection, preservation, restoration, beneficial use and
management of primarily;

(1)        plants,
animals and natural communities that represent diversity of life on Earth by
protecting the lands and waters they need to survive, and secondarily:

(2)        areas
of scientific, historical, cultural, scenic and compatible outdoor recreational
value;

(b)        to
promote such charitable activities or endeavors, including the acquisition,
management and disposal of land and interests in land, as may in the opinion of
the Society board of directors appear to contribute to the above objectives;

(c)        To
encourage co-operation in, support for and research into, and education
regarding all matters pertaining to the fulfillment of the above objectives;

(d)        to do all such
other things as are incidental or ancillary to the attainment of the purposes
and the exercise of the powers of [TLC].

[
9
]

Since 1996, TLC has protected over 250
properties by securing those properties and transferring them to other land
trusts or government park departments or agencies. By 2013, TLC had also
secured and was holding 50 other properties in addition to having secured
approximately 250 conservations covenants on various properties which it
monitors in terms of ensuring compliance with those covenants.

[
10
]

Historically, TLC obtained funding from a
variety of sources, including: private or community foundations, individual
donations, membership dues, other land trusts, corporate donations, gaming
commission money, government grants, community collectives and event and direct
product sales. In some instances, TLC obtained mortgage funding in order to
obtain certain properties quickly where there was urgent need for protection or
in anticipation of later funding which unfortunately never materialized. Funding
from the usual sources, including government agencies, has dropped
significantly over the last few years.

[
11
]

The financial difficulties that arose were first
formally addressed by TLC beginning in 2009 and various restructuring options
were explored. However, these efforts did not garner any significant success.
By early 2012, some of the mortgages were in default and foreclosure
proceedings were commenced. Remittances to Canada Revenue Agency were also in
arrears. TLC was also, by this time, unable to fund the management of its
portfolio of covenants.

[
12
]

TLC’s problems were compounded by various
restrictions as to how they could deal with the various properties. TLC’s
Bylaws set out certain powers and actions the TLC Board of directors may
exercise in respect of property owned by TLC. In particular, the Bylaws contemplated
that properties could be designated as “inalienable” and that once designated,
TLC was prohibited from mortgaging or selling that property save in certain
limited circumstances. Over half of the 50 properties were so designated. These
provisions were designed to enhance the permanence of these conservation
efforts but they have also largely hamstrung TLC in finding a solution to its
financial woes.

[
13
]

As of October 2013, TLC owed in excess of $7.5
million to its secured and unsecured creditors. The value of TLC’s properties
exceeds $43.7 million.

The
CCAA
Proceedings

[
14
]

On October 7, 2013, TLC sought creditor
protection pursuant to the
CCAA
.

[
15
]

One of the first issues addressed was whether
TLC could, as a society, seek protection under the
CCAA
. The
CCAA

applies to a “debtor company” (
s. 3
). Section 2 defines debtor company as a
“company” and “company” is defined as meaning and including:

… any company,
corporation or legal person incorporated by or under an Act of Parliament or of
the legislature of a province, any incorporated company having assets or doing
business in Canada, wherever incorporated …

[
16
]

The
Society Act
, s. 2 provides that
a society may be “incorporated” under that
Act
. Further, s. 4 of
that
Act
provides:

Effect of incorporation

4 (
1)   From the date of the certificate of incorporation, the members
of a society are members of a corporation

(a)   with the name contained in the certificate,

(b)   having perpetual succession,

(c)   with the right to a seal, and

(d)   with the powers
and capacity of a natural person of full capacity as may be required to pursue
its purposes.

[
17
]

In similar circumstances, the Ontario courts
have granted protection to a society under the
CCAA
:
Canadian Red
Cross Society (Re)
,
1998 CanLII 14907 (ON CTGD)
, [1998] O.J. No. 3306 (Ct. J. (Gen.Div.)), leave to
appeal to ONCA refused
1998 CanLII 17737 (ON CA)
, [1998] O.J. No. 6562. Although in a different
context, this court has recognized the status of a society as that of a
corporation:
International Taoist Church of Canada v. Ching Chung Taoist
Association of Hong Kong Limited
,
2010 BCSC 1164
at para.
23
, rev’d on
other grounds
2011 BCCA 149
.

[
18
]

On the basis of these authorities and a plain
reading of the legislation, I was satisfied that as a society, TLC was able to
seek creditor protection under the
CCAA
and on October 7, 2013, this
Court granted an Initial Order (the “Initial Order”). At that time, TLC’s
stated intention was to restructure its operations, assets and affairs to
enable it to continue its conservation efforts and fulfill TLC’s general
purposes as a land trust in British Columbia. The restructuring was intended to
be accomplished through a reduction in operating costs, retirement or
restructuring its debt, growing its membership and funding and perhaps most
importantly, adopting a more entrepreneurial model that would see a more secure
basis for funding of its properties. Critical to this plan was the sale or
transfer of its land holdings to the extent possible in order to eliminate debt
and fund its ongoing operating and restructuring efforts. The Initial Order requires
that this Court approve any sale of TLC’s properties, including the Binning
House.

[
19
]

The Initial Order provided for the appointment
of Wolrige Mahon Limited as Monitor. An Administration Charge of $500,000 and a
Directors’ Charge of $500,000 were approved at that time. In addition, interim
financing in the amount of $1.85 million was approved in order to fund TLC
during the restructuring proceedings and these funds were secured by a DIP
Lenders’ Charge. All of these charges were secured against eight separate
properties of TLC which mostly include those identified by the Monitor as
“heritage properties which have varying degrees of marketability and have
special interest group support that is dedicated to ensure each property’s
special character is maintained and preserved”. One of the properties which was
made subject to the charges under the Initial Order is the Binning House.

[
20
]

On November 4, 2013, this Court extended the
Initial Order and at the time of the hearing, the stay of proceedings was to
expire on January 20, 2014. Since then, the stay has been further extended to
the end of April 2014.

[
21
]

At least two other properties are for sale,
although both are subject to mortgages and any equity realized is not expected
to be sufficient to materially advance TLC’s efforts to restructure. As such, TLC
urgently requires funding in order to move forward with its restructuring
efforts. While opponents of the sale have decried the “monetization” of the
Binning House to satisfy TLC’s creditors, this is a simplistic and to some
extent inaccurate description of what is intended. TLC has been using credit to
support its conservancy efforts, which include those relating to Binning House.

[
22
]

In addition, if TLC is to survive its financial
difficulties and continue with its conservation efforts, it must have the
ability to fund the continuation of this proceeding under the
CCAA
. In
that sense, obtaining these sale proceeds represents a key part of ensuring the
attainment of these laudable goals. Accordingly, the fate of TLC is somewhat
linked to the Binning House and the reverse is also true; the fate of the
Binning House is somewhat linked to the fate of TLC.

The Binning House

[
23
]

The Binning House is located in West Vancouver.
It was designed and constructed in 1941 by Bertram Charles (B.C.) Binning, a well-known
Canadian artist. Since its construction and continuing to this day, it has been
recognized as one of the first and finest examples of the West Coast modern
architectural movement. For that reason, since its construction, the Binning
House was seen as having significant cultural and heritage value, both
nationally and locally and it remains so to this day.

[
24
]

On the death of B.C. Binning in 1976, the
Binning House passed to his widow, Jessie Binning.

[
25
]

The Binning House was designated a national
historic site of Canada on March 12, 1998.

[
26
]

In 1999, the District of West Vancouver (the “District”)
passed certain bylaws (the “Bylaws”) at the request of Jessie Binning, being Heritage
Designation Bylaw No. 4157, 1999, designating the Binning House as a
Municipal Heritage site and Heritage Maintenance Bylaw No. 4187, 1999,
establishing maintenance standards for Heritage Designated Buildings and Sites.
Title to the Binning House references a notation as to the Notice of Heritage
Status.

[
27
]

The Designation Bylaw sets out the components
and features of the Binning House designated for heritage protection, the
requirement that the Binning House be “maintained in good order” in accordance
with the Maintenance Bylaw, and the requirement to seek authorization of the District’s
Director of Planning and Development in order to make any changes to the
interior or exterior finishes not otherwise permitted by the Bylaws.

[
28
]

In 2007, Jessie Binning passed away without any
direct heirs. Details of her last will are in issue on this application, as
discussed below.

[
29
]

Through a series of transactions in 2008, which
will be discussed in more detail below, the executors of Jessie Binning’s
estate (the “Estate”) began working with TLC to ensure that the Binning House
would be preserved into the future. The process that was agreed upon involved
the setting up of a separate society called the Binning Heritage Property
Society (“BHPS”).

[
30
]

On October 16, 2008, title to the Binning House
was transferred from the Estate to this new society and immediately thereafter,
BHPS transferred the Binning House to TLC. A Deed of Gift was also executed by
both BHPS and TLC at the same time.

[
31
]

Since that time, the Binning House has been
administered by TLC as one of the many properties under its control and it has
been dealt with in accordance with its general purposes. In particular, all
revenue relating to the Binning House has been deposited into its general
operating account and all disbursements have been paid from this same account
although TLC maintained operating budgets specifically relating to the
property. Unlike some of its properties, TLC never designated the Binning House
as “inalienable”.

[
32
]

In the period of approximately five years since
TLC took title to the Binning House, the Binning House has been available for
public viewing and public use from time to time, either through guided tours,
open houses or special events.

[
33
]

The only charges against Binning House are the charges
granted in the Initial Order, as noted above.

[
34
]

In October 2011, TLC arranged for a tenant or warden
to reside in the Binning House to provide security and assist in minor
maintenance and facilitate any tours, events and workshops there. The warden
has been paying $700 per month in rent to TLC which has been deposited into
TLC’s general revenue.

[
35
]

TLC has completed only minor maintenance and no
capital improvements to the Binning House since it was acquired in 2008.

The Sale Agreement

[
36
]

On October 28, 2013, TLC received an
unsolicited offer from BJW Real Estate Holdings Ltd. (“BJW”) to purchase the
Binning House for $1.6 million, subject only to the Bylaws. The offer included
all personal property on the premises, including: artwork, drawings and
furniture associated with B.C. and Jessie Binning. The offer initially contemplated
a closing at the end of November 2013.

[
37
]

It was later revealed that the person behind the
BJW offer was in fact Bruno Wall, a Vancouver businessman. Mr. Wall has
been collecting the works of B.C. Binning for over ten years and has
accumulated a significant collection to date. As such, he clearly has an
interest in acquiring this large “work” of B.C. Binning. Mr. Wall’s offer
requires that title to the Binning House be transferred to him free of any
trust or other requirements.

[
38
]

After inspecting the Binning House, BJW obtained
the services of an engineer to determine the condition of it. The engineering report
obtained by BJW indicates that Binning House is in a “structurally satisfactory
condition” but it requires some repairs and a “regular building maintenance
program”. The engineer estimated that $150,000 to $200,000 would be required for
those repairs, to prevent further structural deterioration and to ensure
compliance with the Bylaws. BJW or Mr. Wall has the financial resources to
have this work performed.

[
39
]

Mr. Wall has indicated that he will review
all reasonable proposals for public access and educational purposes once the
property is restored.

[
40
]

The offer exceeds the 2013 assessed value of
Binning House in the amount of $1,519,900. In December 2012, TLC had received
another unsolicited offer in the amount of $700,000. In addition, based on the
valuation information gathered by TLC indicating a range of
$1,775,000-$1,825,000, TLC is satisfied that the offer represents fair market
value.

[
41
]

On the basis of the above, TLC decided that the
offer was a provident one and the offer was accepted, subject to court
approval. In particular and in light of its stated purpose under its Constitution,
TLC was of the view that BJW/Mr. Wall was a suitable and appropriate
purchaser for the Binning House since Mr. Wall was expected to preserve
and protect the Binning House in accordance with the Bylaws.

[
42
]

Further, TLC is of the view that the sale of the
Binning House would further the goals of its restructuring efforts by divesting
it and freeing up necessary funds to facilitate these
CCAA
proceedings. Retaining
the Binning House is not essential to TLC’s restructuring goals.

[
43
]

In anticipation of the sale, TLC has now given the
warden notice to vacate the premises by the end of January 2014.

[
44
]

At the November 4, 2013 hearing, counsel for TLC
referred to the conditionally accepted offer to purchase and that an
application would be brought on quickly to obtain the necessary court approval.
By that time, however, opposition to the sale was beginning to mount. At the
return of the application on November 18, 2013, BHPS was not present; however,
substantial others interests, including the District, were aligned against
TLC’s sale of the Binning House. Alternatively, if the sale was approved, the
University of British Columbia (“UBC”), a beneficiary under the will in
question, asserted that it was entitled to the proceeds of the sale. The
Attorney General of British Columbia (the “AG”) indicated her intention to
provide the court with assistance on the trust issues raised and generally
speaking, the AG submitted that TLC did not hold beneficial interest in the Binning
House that could be sold.

[
45
]

The arguments against the sale raise substantial
issues relating to TLC’s right to deal with the Binning House in light of the
potential application of the
CPPA
and general trust law and issues
relating to the interpretation of Jessie Binning’s will. Before I address those
issues, I will briefly address the issue in relation to this sale under the
CCAA
.

[
46
]

Section 36
of the
CCAA
provides:

Restriction on disposition of business
assets

36.
(1)   A
debtor company in respect of which an order has been made under this Act may
not sell or otherwise dispose of assets outside the ordinary course of business
unless authorized to do so by a court. Despite any requirement for shareholder
approval, including one under federal or provincial law, the court may
authorize the sale or disposition even if shareholder approval was not
obtained.

…

Factors to be considered

(3)   In deciding whether to grant the
authorization, the court is to consider, among other things,

(
a
)  whether
the process leading to the proposed sale or disposition was reasonable in the
circumstances;

(
b
)  whether
the monitor approved the process leading to the proposed sale or disposition;

(
c
)  whether
the monitor filed with the court a report stating that in their opinion the
sale or disposition would be more beneficial to the creditors than a sale or
disposition under a bankruptcy;

(
d
)  the
extent to which the creditors were consulted;

(
e
)  the
effects of the proposed sale or disposition on the creditors and other
interested parties; and

(
f
)   whether the consideration to be
received for the assets is reasonable and fair, taking into account their
market value.

[
47
]

There are obviously some factors set out in
s. 36(3) which make this proposed sale somewhat unusual. First and
foremost, this offer was unsolicited and therefore, there was no “process” by
which it was obtained in order to test the market for its value. This point is
somewhat muted by the fact that this proposed sale has now been covered
extensively in the press since November 2013, although I will return to this matter
in relation to the trust issues. Despite some suggestion during the hearing
that another offer might materialize, I am advised that no other offeror has
come forward.

[
48
]

In any event, the offer exceeds the assessed
price and TLC’s efforts to determine value has confirmed the reasonableness of
the amount, particularly in light of the repairs that need to be done to the
Binning House.

[
49
]

Secondly, general creditors have not been
consulted. No secured creditors have mortgages against title. The DIP Lenders
support the sale. Assuming that the offer represents fair market value, there
is obvious benefit to the general creditors in shedding an asset which results
in a cash drain and which results in the monetization of the Binning House for
TLC’s urgent financing needs.

[
50
]

Finally and importantly, the Monitor has fully
reviewed the situation and fully supports the sale in accordance with its
Second Report to Court on November 14, 2013. The Monitor supports the assertion
of TLC that the offer is at fair market value and that its sale is provident at
this time in terms of freeing up badly needed operating funds for not only the
restructuring process but its continuing mandate to protect its various property
interests. Indeed, since the fall of 2013, TLC’s funding needs have become more
acute and it appears that ongoing operations are only possible because
professional fees are not being paid when incurred.

[
51
]

The Monitor notes that TLC has been funding the
management of the Binning House from its general operating funds since, despite
its initial intentions, it did not obtain any funding specifically for the
purpose of maintaining and preserving the Binning House. Despite having been
granted some property tax relief from the District and having received various
specific grants over the years, the Monitor also notes that TLC does not have
the financial capability to manage, maintain and preserve the Binning House into
the future.

[
52
]

No person has asserted that the statutory test
in
s. 36
of the
CCAA
has not been met on the evidence.

[
53
]

Accordingly, at the outset and in these unusual
circumstances, I am satisfied that, assuming that the Binning House is TLC’s
“asset” available for disposition by it (i.e. subject to the will and
CPPA
/trust
issues discussed below), a sale of the Binning House is appropriate at this
time.

The Issues

[
54
]

The issues are:

a)

The Will Issue
: did Jessie Binning’s
will allow the transfer of the Binning House to BHPS and then to TLC?

b)

The Trust Issues
:

i.

does the
CPPA
or general trust law apply
so as to prevent the sale of the Binning House by TLC on the proposed terms?

ii.

if the Binning House is subject to a statutory or common law trust
in the hands of TLC, should the trust be modified?

iii.

in any event, is the Binning House exigible by TLC’s creditors?

Summary of the Evidence

[
55
]

As stated above, Jessie Binning died in May 2007
leaving her last will and testament dated February 15, 2007 (the “Will”). The
executors and trustees under her Will were Geoffrey Massey, Ronald Patrick
Walsh and Everhard Van Lidth de Jeude (the “Executors”).

[
56
]

The Will at para. 4(g)(i) stated at the
outset that the Binning House had been designated a National Heritage Site and
was listed on the heritage inventory of the District. Paragraph 4(g) continued:

(ii)        it
is my hope that the [Binning House] and historic household furnishings will be
preserved for historical purposes;

(iii)       if
my Trustees decide it is feasible and practical to do so, to establish a
foundation or other organization, society, association or corporation (the
“Entity”), as my Trustees decide, and to transfer any interest … I have in the
[Binning House], along with those household furnishings selected by my
Trustees, to the Entity to hold, maintain and use the [Binning House] and those
household furnishings for those purposes it decides are desirable;

(iv)       if
the [Binning House] is transferred to the Entity and, due to unforeseen
circumstances, the Entity decides it is no longer feasible or practical to
retain the [Binning House] and it subsequently sells the [Binning House], it is
my hope that it will give the net sale proceeds to the
B.C. BINNING MEMORIAL
FELLOWSHIP FUND
, administered by
THE UNIVERSITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
,
for the purpose of creating additional scholarships to be awarded by it each
year from the income earned by those proceeds;

(v)        if
my Trustees decide not to retain the [Binning House] and historic household
furnishings, the Trustees will sell the [Binning House], and sell or otherwise
dispose of those household furnishings, and give the net sale proceeds to the
B.C.
BINNING MEMORIAL FELLOWSHIP FUND
, for the purpose of creating additional
scholarships to be awarded by it each year from the income earned by those
proceeds;

[Emphasis in original]

[
57
]

Paragraph 4 of the Will further dealt with the residue
of the estate funds:

(l)         If
the Entity is established pursuant to paragraph 4.(g)(iii) of this Will, to
divide the residue of my estate between the Entity and the
B.C. BINNING
MEMORIAL FELLOWSHIP FUND
, in such portions (including giving the entire residue
to one of them to the exclusion of the other), as my Trustees decide;

(m)      If
the Entity is not established pursuant to paragraph 4.(g)(iii) of this Will, to
give the residue of my estate to the
B.C. BINNING MEMORIAL FELLOWSHIP FUND
.

[Emphasis in original]

[
58
]

In late 2007, the Executors and TLC had
discussions regarding whether TLC could take over ownership of the Binning
House in accordance with the terms of the Will. Mr. Massey, one of the

(i)         Interpretation of the
Will

[
92
]

The general rules of interpretation of wills
begin with determining the intention of the testator based on the natural and
ordinary meaning of the words used, as set out in
National Trust Co. Ltd. v.
Fleury
,
1965 CanLII 18 (SCC)
, [1965
]
S.C.R. 817 at 829:

In the
construction of wills, the primary purpose is to determine the intention of the
testator and it is only when such intention cannot be arrived at with
reasonable certainty by giving the natural and ordinary meaning to the words
which he has used that resort is to be had to the rules of construction which
have been developed by the Courts in the interpretation of other wills.

[
93
]

One must look at the entire will and not simply
read provisions in isolation: “[t]he testator’s intention is to be gathered
from a consideration of the will as a whole and not solely from the words used,
say, in an unclear portion of the will. … the testator’s intention is to be
ascertained, first of all, from the four corners of the will”: James MacKenzie,

Feeney’s Canadian Law of Wills
, loose-leaf (consulted on 16 December
2013), (Markham, ON: LexisNexis Canada, 2000), at para. 10.60.

[
94
]

Where the testator has used a word which can
have only one reasonable meaning in the circumstances, the court cannot assume
that the testator would have had a different intention: MacKenzie at para. 10.44.

[
95
]

If the intention of the testator can be
construed in the context of the will as a whole, it is not necessary to look
any further:
Smith v. Smith Estate
,
2010 BCCA 106
at para.
18
.

[
96
]

If it is not possible to construe the intention based
on the document alone due to some ambiguity, the court may have resort to what
has been called the “armchair rule” in order to try to resolve the ambiguity.
This is explained by MacKenzie at para. 10.45:

In the first
instance, the court may not be convinced that the testator’s intention can be
discerned from the will itself. In such a situation, since the testator must be
taken to have used the language of the will in view of the surrounding
circumstances known to him or her when he or she made his or her will, evidence
of such circumstances is necessarily admissible, at least insofar as it
corresponds to the facts and circumstances referred to in the will.

[
97
]

What constitutes the types of evidence of “surrounding
circumstances” that may, or may not be, looked at when interpreting a will was
discussed in
Murray Estate
,
2007 BCSC 1035
at paras.
7-12
. At para. 7,
the court stated:

When construing
the terms of a will, the court may look to the surrounding circumstances existing
at the time the will was made to determine the testator's intention. The court
may not, however, have regard to direct extrinsic evidence of intent, except in
limited circumstances, as the will is presumed to have been accepted by the
testator, and to speak for itself. That rule applies, in particular, to
instructions provided to his solicitor.

[
98
]

or

make, or fix firmly; to enact permanently <one object of the Constitution

2
.
To make or form; to bring about or
into existence

courts>.

[Emphasis in
UBC’s submissions

that goes considerably beyond the actual words found in the Will. Specifically,

and practical
to fund and manage an entity
to hold the Binning House”
[emphasis
a

the Entity

104

Estate of Cecil Charles Herbert Holmes
,

2007
BCSC 51
at para.
15
and
Daradick v. McKeand Estate
,
2012 ONSC 5622

at para.
40
, the courts did consider that in those circumstances, prior

[
105
]

a)         December 19, 2001: which gave broad discretion to the Executors
to enter into arrangements with governments or private organizations to

b)         February 7, 2004: which directed the Executors to

[
106

[
107

I accept TLC’s argument that the final version of the Will is the
document that I must consider and not prior unsigned draft wills. The argument
that draft wills are admissible as evidence of intention is akin to looking at
instructions given to a solicitor, which this court expressly stated is
impermissible to determine intention, per
Murray Estate
at para.
7
.
Further, this is analogous to contracts, where the signed contract is the
relevant version and previous unsigned versions do not assist to ascertain
intention. Intention may change over time and what is relevant is the intention
evident at the time of signing of the last will.

[
108
]

The other material relied on by UBC includes an email just before
execution of the February 2004 will sent by Jessie Binning’s lawyer who indicated

purpose feasible.” In September 2005, Mr. Walsh, one of the Executors, commented
that Mrs. Binning wanted her trustees to have significant discretion
regarding the Binning House and that she was aware that it might not be
practical to maintain the house and that it would probably have to be sold. To
the extent that UBC relies on this further evidence as evidence of Jessie
Binning’s intention, it is inadmissible. It is not evidence of the “surrounding
circumstances” relating to the execution of the Will:
Daradick
,

para.
40
.
In addition, the comments are hearsay and are not even attributable to Jessie
Binning. As such, none of this further evidence has any probative value or
relevance in any event in determining Jessie Binning’s intentions in February
2007, some years later. The same can be said with even greater force with respect
to the various handwritten notes, where one is not even dated and the author is
not identified in either of them.

[
109
]

Accordingly, the only relevant and admissible evidence advanced by
UBC are the three prior signed wills.

[
110
]

UBC argues that the previous wills are evidence of Jessie Binning’s intention
that the Executors would preserve the Binning House under the “auspices of a
society or foundation established” by them. UBC also submits that the previous
wills establish Jessie Binning’s understanding that her estate may not have
sufficient funds to fund the Entity and that in that event, she intended that
the Executors sell the Binning House and pay the proceeds to UBC. In
particular, UBC argues that the change in her February 2004 will - that the
Executors establish an “Entity” - is indicative that she wished to ensure that
the entity was one established and controlled by the Executors and was funded
by her estate in accordance with the residue clause.

[
111
]

Again, I am unable to accept UBC’s restrictive interpretation of the
Will. As I have stated above, Jessie Binning’s Will granted considerable
discretion to the Executors. I agree that the residue clause does indicate that
she intended to fund, if possible, the Entity, if it was established. However,
on a reasonable interpretation of the Will, the Executors’ discretion to
establish the Entity and deal with the Binning House was not fettered by a
precondition that sufficient funds would be available from the estate to hold
and manage the Binning House in a separate society controlled by the Executors in
perpetuity.

[
112
]

Even if UBC is correct that the earlier wills (and some or all of
the other extrinsic evidence) indicate that Jessie Binning had concerns about
the ability of her estate to fund the Entity, it remains the case that from
2005, the discretion afforded to the Executors was restricted only the
pre-condition that they decide whether it was “feasible and practical”. She
died only 3 months after execution of the Will. Knowing what she did about the
value of her estate, had she wished to restrict the Executors as UBC suggests,
it would have been open to her to say as much in the Will. Rather, I take the
late expression of her intention in the Will to “preserve” the Binning House as
confirmation of her intention to allow the Executors as much flexibility as
possible in attempting to achieve that purpose.

[
113
]

In conclusion, based on an interpretation of the Will itself, I find
that Jessie Binning’s intention was to preserve the Binning House into the
future. The Binning House was not just a house or residence to Jessie Binning.
By the time of its construction, the Binnings had been married for some six
years and after it was constructed, the Binnings used the house for the next 35
years, until B.C. Binning’s death, as a salon and showcase for B.C. Binning’s
considerable artistic talents. Jessie Binning resided in this house for some 56
years in total. She knew that this house was a great achievement of her husband
and that it was of great cultural significance.

[
114
]

In that regard, Jessie Binning gave the Executors significant
discretion towards achieving the purpose of preserving the property in relation
to establishing an Entity in accordance with paragraph 4(g)(iii) of the Will.
That discretion was not fettered in the sense of requiring that the Executors
determine, as a precondition to the exercise of their discretion, that the Estate
would have sufficient resources to fund the Entity’s operations in perpetuity
and that the Executors were prepared to maintain control over the Entity for
that purpose. Even if there is some ambiguity in the Will in that respect, I
consider that the further evidence of the surrounding circumstances, being the
prior wills, does not detract from that interpretation and in fact supports it.

(ii)        Fraud on a Power

[
115
]

The thrust of UBC’s argument on the interpretation of the Will is that
the Executors acted outside the scope of their powers under the Will in
benefiting TLC as a “non-object” and as such committed a fraud on the power.
UBC argues that given the fraud on a power, the dispositions of the Binning
House to BHPS and subsequently to TLC are void.

[
116
]

TLC argues that the Executors acted with proper authority when they
established BHPS and then transferred the Binning House to BHPS. TLC submits
that “[o
]
nce the Binning House was transferred to the BHPS, any claim UBC may
have to the Binning House or proceeds of sale thereof is based on a ‘hope’ of
Jessie Binning.” This argument is said to flow directly from the language set
out in paragraph 4(g)(iv) of Jessie Binning’s Will.

[
117
]

UBC and TLC agree that the two basic elements of fraud on a power are
set out in Geraint Thomas
, Thomas on Powers
, 2d ed. (Oxford: Oxford
University Press, 2012) at para. 9.02:

a)         a disposition that is beyond the scope of the power, with
reference to the terms of the instrument; and

b)         a deliberate breach of the implied obligation not to
exercise the power for an ulterior purpose.

[
118
]

While the doctrine of fraud on a power has an ancient history from
English common law, there is scarce jurisprudence on the topic from other parts
of the Commonwealth.

[
119
]

Both parties principally relied on case
authorities from New Zealand, which I will discuss below. The only Canadian
case referred to me was
Edell v. Sitzer
,
2001 CanLII 27989 (ON SC)
, [2001] O.J. No. 2909 (S.C.J.),
aff’d
2004 CanLII 654 (ON CA)
, [2004] O.J. No. 2314 (C.A.). In the lower court, Cullity J. sets out
the doctrine per Snell’s
Principles of Equity
, 29th ed. (London: Sweet
& Maxwell, 1990), pp. 562-63:

[164]    …The
donee of a special power of appointment must exercise the power bona fide and
for the end designed and not for any purpose which is foreign to the power. If
the power is exercised not bona fide, but for a purpose beyond the scope of the
instrument creating the power, or not justified by it, the appointment is said
to be a fraud on the power, and equity holds it bad.

[
120
]

The question of whether there has been a fraud on a power (or to put
it another way, the exercise of that power for an improper purpose) must have
regard to the true intentions of the donor of the power as to its scope and purpose:
Thomas, para. 9.03. As Thomas similarly notes, at para. 9.01, “the
power can be exercised only in favour of the objects of that power and in
furtherance of the purpose for which it was conferred”.

[
121
]

Thomas at paras. 9.01-02 states that the
concept is a “slippery” or “difficult” one and that is more than evident from a
reading of the case authorities, particularly from New Zealand. Thomas notes that
a “fraudulent exercise of a power”, such as UBC alleges here, must be
distinguished from simply an “excessive execution” of a power:

… The dividing line can sometimes be
difficult to discern, but
what is of decisive importance is the intention or
purpose of the donee in exercising the power
: if there is present some
‘ulterior purpose’ or ‘collateral purpose’, a ‘deliberate defeating’ of the
donor’s intention, there is a fraud on the power. An
excessive
execution
of a power generally turns on a question of construction. A
fraudulent

execution turns upon the true intention or real motive of the donee of the
power, which is usually much more difficult to ascertain (Thomas at para. 9.02).

[Emphasis
added].

[
122
]

If there is a fraud on a power and the trustees attempted to use a
power they did not possess, then this court must not come to the rescue “by
treating their action as if they had been engaged in exercising a quite
different power that they did actually possess”:
Kain v. Hutton
, [2008
]

NZSC 61 at para. 35. As Tipping J. stated in his concurring judgment, the
donee “is acting pursuant to a mandate granted by the donor of the power and
must stay within that mandate”:
Kain
at para. 46.

[
123
]

Similar to how the courts have characterized a
“fraud” in the context of fraudulent conveyances, the use of the word “fraud”
here also does not necessarily have any sinister meaning. In
Vatcher v.
Paull
,
[1915] AC 372 at 378,
the Privy Council explained fraud on a power:

The term fraud
in connection with frauds on a power does not necessarily denote any conduct on
the part of the appointor amounting to fraud in the common law meaning of the
term or any conduct which could be properly termed dishonest or immoral. It
merely means that the power has been exercised for a purpose, or with an intention,
beyond the scope of or not justified by the instrument creating the power.

[
124
]

The onus of proving that there was a fraud on a power rests on the
party asserting it:
Kain
, para. 19. It is agreed that if a fraud on
the power is found, the execution of that power is void: Thomas, para. 9.90;

Re Marsden’s Trust
(1859), 4 Drew 594 at 601.

[
125
]

UBC submits that the Executors acted in fraud on
a power as they were aware that “TLC was a non-object and they exercised their
power intentionally to benefit that non-object.” UBC says that the Executors
improperly used BHPS as a “flow through entity” with the sole intention of
benefiting TLC, who was not an object under the terms of the Will. This
argument was largely predicated on UBC’s interpretation argument above, which I
have rejected. This led to UBC’s submissions that since there was no money in
the Estate to fund the Entity, a sale of the Binning House was the only option
available to the Executors. I agree with TLC that UBC’s unacceptable argument
is:

predicated on
the assumption that, for the power to be validly exercised, the “Entity”, as
such term is defined in the Will, was required to “hold, maintain and use” the
Binning House in such a way that precluded later alienation, and the Trustees
were required to intend that the Entity so “hold, maintain and use” without
possibility of alienation.

[
126
]

Nevertheless, assuming my interpretation of the Will is correct, I
will further consider UBC’s argument in the context of whether the Executors’ intentions
were such that they deliberately exercised their discretion for an improper
purpose given the arrangements with BHPS.

[
127
]

As noted above, the matter must first be
considered with reference to the testator’s true intentions, in accordance with
the language in the Will, as to the scope and purpose of the powers given to
the Executors. George Farwell
states:

Any attempt to
exceed the limitations of the power through the medium of any appointment to
one of the objects of it in exclusion of the others, is equally invalid,
whether the purpose of the donee be selfish, or, as he supposes, a more
beneficial mode of effecting that which he takes the donor of the power to have
desired. The Court will not allow him to interpret the donor’s intention in any
other sense than the Court itself holds to be the true construction of the
instrument creating the power; and a literal execution of the power, with a purpose
which it does not sanction, is regarded as a fraud on the power (George
Farwell,
A Concise Treatise on Powers
, 2d ed. (London, UK: Stevens and
Sons Ltd.,1893) at 404 (HeinOnline)).

[
128
]

Professor Waters also demonstrates the importance of the testator’s
intention: “[w]hat the testator intended is clearly a question of construction
of his language, and no case on construction is a binding precedent for a later
case, but this does not deprive precedent of significance, and it is impossible
to read these cases without realising that other judges could have reached
different results” (Donovan W.M. Waters, Q.C., ed.,
Waters’ Law of Trusts in
Canada
, 3d ed. (Toronto: Thomson Carswell, 2005) at 98).

[
129
]

Farwell and Waters’ commentary reiterates that Jessie Binning’s
intention must be ascertained through the wording of her Will. From her
intention, this court can determine whether the Executors
exceeded any limitations in the exercise of their
discretion that she intended.

[
130
]

I have already discussed above that considerable discretion was
given to the Executors in terms of the
scope
of the powers granted. It
is also abundantly clear that the
purpose
of the exercise of the powers
granted to the Executors was as stated in paragraph 4(g)(ii) of the Will;
namely, to preserve the Binning House for historical purposes.

[
131
]

Therefore, in this context, the next question that must be decided
is whether the Executors were able to exercise their discretion as they did
and

did they have an improper intention to benefit TLC, a non-object under the
Will?

[
132
]

Thomas identifies various grounds or categories upon which the
exercise of a power may be fraudulent. Two are relevant here and are of
assistance in framing the issues: (1) if made pursuant to an antecedent
agreement or bargain between the donee (the Executors) and an object of the
power whereby a non-object is to benefit or (2) for a purpose “foreign” to the
power: para. 9.13. In the context of UBC’s arguments, the first category
is really a subset of the second.

[
133
]

Under the first category, the issue is whether there was an
agreement or bargain between the Executors and BHPS/TLC regarding the Binning House. In
Vatcher
, at 378
this was said to be perhaps the most common instance of a fraud on a power.

[
134
]

The courts have said that a fraud may occur where there has been
some bargain between the donor and the donee, where the donor himself is to
derive a benefit, or as the Privy Council stated “[i]t is enough that the
appointor’s purpose and intention is to secure a benefit for himself, or some
other person not an object of the power”:
Vatcher
at 378; see also

Kain
at para. 18; and
Wong v. Burt
, [2004] NZCA 174 at para. 29.

[
135
]

However, in
Kain
, Tipping J. explained that this “classic”
statement cannot be applied “in those literal terms and in isolation of the
rationale of the doctrine. … The focus should rather be on whether the purpose
of the appointment was truly to benefit an object. If that is so, it does not
matter that a non-object also obtains a benefit”:
Kain
at paras. 48-49;
Farwell at 409-10. Indeed, the court in
Vatcher
at 379 states “[i]t is
not enough that the appointor or some person not an object of the power may
conceivably derive some benefit”.

[
136
]

Thomas makes two key points on this sub issue:

a)         the mere existence of an agreement or bargain between the appointor
and the appointee is not enough to void the appointment; rather, it must be
shown that, but for the agreement or bargain, the appointment would not have
been made (para. 9.16);
and

b)         it does not follow that an appointment to an object of
the power, coupled with a contemporaneous settlement by that object of the
appointed fund to a non-object, is automatically void (para. 9.15).

[
137
]

In
Goldsmid v. Goldsmid
,
(1842) 2 Hare
187
, the mother had received a gift under a power and passed some of it on to
her son, which was held to be valid. In
Goldsmid
, the Vice-Chancellor
found at 198:

In the simple
case where there has been nothing more than the concurrence of the donee of the
power and one of the objects of the power, to whom an exclusive appointment
might be made, or to whom an appointment might be made co-extensive with the
amount of the property disposed of, the Court has treated the appointment as
valid and effectual.

[
138
]

The Vice-Chancellor went on to say at 198:

… where the
appointee, an object of the power, joins in the deed of appointment, and the
deed shows that that which is done has been so done by agreement with that
party, the Court considers that party as making a settlement of the property.
If
Ann
, therefore, to whom unquestionably an exclusive appointment might
have been made, agrees that the property shall be make (sic) whether the
property is given to
Ann
in the form of an interest, or whether a
control over the property is given to
Ann
in the form of a power. The
act complained of is not, according to the construction of the cases, the act
of the donee of the power, but it is the separate act of
Ann
, which she
acquired the power of exercising by means of the appointment first made by the
donees of the power.

[
139
]

Referring to
Goldsmid
, Farwell states
that “[t]he mere existence of a contract between appointor and appointee for a
settlement is not enough to avoid the appointment. In order to do this, it must
be shown that the contract induced the appointment, and that, but for the
contract, the appointment would not have been made” (Farwell at 419). Farwell
further says:

And the donee of
a limited power of appointment may well execute it in favour of an object of
the power, though he believes and knows that the appointee will at once dispose
of the property in favour of
persons who are not objects of the power. But if, besides this belief and
knowledge, there is a bargain between the appointor and appointee that the
appointee shall make a disposition in favour of persons not objects of the
power, and the just result of the evidence is that the appointment would not
have been made but for the bargain, then the appointment is void (at 418).

[
140
]

Both of Thomas’ points were raised and addressed
in
Kain
. In that case, the trustees had discretion to encroach on
capital to pay Mrs. Couper (the widow) or certain children of the
testator’s sister’s children. Certain shares were transferred to Mrs. Couper
who then immediately settled those shares in a trust whose beneficiaries
included her children, who were admittedly not objects under the original
trust. Similar to this case, the other beneficiaries argued that Mrs. Couper
was simply a “conduit” used for the purpose of benefiting non-objects. The
court upheld the transactions, noting that the purpose of the appointment was
to benefit Mrs. Couper and that the immediate settling of the trust by her
did not detract from that purpose (paras. 19-22). Further, Tipping J.
stated in his concurring judgment:

[49]      The problem with Lord Parker’s
formulation, unless it is understood and applied in the light of the
substantial body of case law which preceded it, is that it has the focus in the
wrong place.
An appointment which secures a benefit for a non-object is not
for that reason alone a fraud on the power. The focus should rather be on
whether the purpose of the appointment was truly to benefit an object. If that
is so, it does not matter that a non-object also obtains a benefit
.

[50]      In
Pilkington
’s case
Viscount Radcliffe suggested that the primary benefit must be to the object,
with the benefit to the non-object being “incidental”.
I agree with what
Thomas says in his work on powers that it seems clear from the cases that the
benefit derived by the non-object need not be merely incidental. That said,
whatever the nature and comparative level of the benefit conferred on the
non-object, the key point is that the purpose of the appointment must truly be
to benefit the object
. Whether that is so should be determined in a broad
way bearing in mind the commercial, conveyancing, family or other realities of
what is occurring.

[51]      The normal rationale for the use
of a special power of appointment is to give to the donee/appointor the ability
to choose, on the donor’s behalf, among a range of potential beneficiaries
nominated by the donor. The power is given because the donor is unlikely to be
able to anticipate all the relevant circumstances, including fiscal considerations,
which will apply at the time the appointment falls to be made. Hence the donor
gives the power to a person or persons whom he trusts to make the selection
when the time comes and when the relevant circumstances are known.

[52]      The appointor may decide that
object A should be the subject of an appointment. Object A is aware of the
proposed appointment. She wants to pass the benefit of the appointment on to a
family trust. She does not want to be left with the conveyancing and potential
gift duty implications of receiving the property herself and then transferring
it to the trust. Provided she is fully informed of her rights and is not
subject to any improper pressure, I consider it would be too narrow a view to
insist on the appointment being made to object A herself, despite her wish to
direct the appointment elsewhere. In these circumstances the appointment is of
benefit to A as well as to the non-objects who take possession.

[53]
In such circumstances, the
appointor, if acceding to A’s request, clearly has the purpose and intention of
benefiting non-objects if the beneficiaries of the family trust are not objects
of the power which the appointor is exercising. But cases of this kind have
never been regarded as caught by the doctrine of fraud on a power. This is
because the direction of A is regarded as justifying the direct appointment to
the family trust, albeit its beneficiaries are non-objects. The rationale for
this view is that such a transaction is not fairly capable of being regarded as
an abuse of the donor’s mandate as it is truly of benefit to A, albeit it is
also of benefit to the beneficiaries of the family trust
.

[54]      Clearly, in the present case, as
Blanchard J’s reasons demonstrate, there was no abuse of the appointor’s
mandate in the appointment of the Ponui shares directly to the Annette Couper
Ponui Trust. The terms of that trust and the circumstances in which Mrs Annette
Couper acquiesced in the appointment being made to the trust rather than to
herself, demonstrate that the appointment was of real benefit to Mrs Couper,
she being an object of the power. It is not a case where the donor of the power
can reasonably complain that the power has been misused. Hence I would reject
the contention that the appointment of the Ponui shares represented a fraud on
the relevant power.

[Emphasis added.
Footnotes removed]

[
141
]

UBC relies in particular on
Wong
. In that
case, the husband died leaving the residuary estate in trust to pay an annual
income to his wife. A power of encroachment was given in favour of the wife.
The will directed that upon the wife’s death, the annual income be paid to
their two daughters and upon the death of the last surviving daughter, the
residue be paid to the children or grandchildren of only one daughter and not
the other due to a falling out in the family. After the husband’s death, the
one daughter also passed away and the wife became concerned for the
grandchildren who were cut out of her husband’s will. As a result, the
trustees, in consultation with the wife and with legal advice, encroached on
the capital and put the money that was removed in a separate trust for the
grandchildren who were cut out of the will. The New Zealand Court of Appeal
found that this was a fraud on a power (paras. 41-42) but also
specifically said at para. 42 that if the wife:

… had simply
been advanced the money out of the estate and had then exercised genuine
freedom of action to benefit the children (as for instance by setting up a
trust for them), that would not have been unlawful. But what was knowingly
erected was a deliberate scheme to subvert the terms of the will. What was
overlooked was that the property was vested in those entitled in default of the
exercise of the power, subject to its being divested by a proper exercise of
the power in clause 6, and the steps in fact taken gave rise to a fraud on
those entitled in default.

[
142
]

In
Wong
, the objects of the power were specific family
members. The discretion that the trustees had was very limited and allowed them
to deal only with those specific objects. While the New Zealand case of
Wong

is instructive regarding the law, the facts in that case can be
distinguished from the facts here.

[
143
]

In contrast, here the Executors had considerable discretion. They had the ability to decide whether
it was “feasible and practical” to establish an Entity. They acted in
accordance with Jessie Binning’s wishes to preserve the Binning House for
historical purposes and they, as they were empowered to do, set up an Entity to
which they transferred the Binning House. At the time of the transfer, the
Executors had no interest in BHPS, and they were not required to have obtained
such a continuing interest.

[
144
]

Immediately upon receiving the transfer of the Binning House, the
directors of BHPS transferred it to TLC, which was also in accordance with
Jessie Binning’s wishes and her intention evidenced in her Will, paragraph
4(g)(iii). The “purposes [BHPS] decide[d were] desirable” were to pass the
Binning House on to TLC, again in keeping with Jessie Binning’s overall intention
of preserving the house for historical purposes.

[
145
]

UBC argues that the transfer by the Executors was a “deliberate
pre-conceived plan to subvert the terms of the Will”. This argument appears to arise
from the evidence of Mr. Massey, one of the Executors, that he and the
other Executors set up an “intermediary society” so as to allow an immediate transfer
of the Binning House to TLC. In its argument, UBC suggests that the Executors’ “plan”
or “purpose” was to “get the Binning House into the hands of TLC”. With
respect, as I alluded to earlier in these reasons, this conflates the distinct
concepts of scope and purpose of the power discussed by Thomas at para. 9.06.

[
146
]

There is little doubt that the Executors established BHPS with the
idea that they would cede control of BHPS to TLC almost immediately. In
addition, despite the initial plan to leave the Binning House in BHPS for ongoing
management by TLC, the Executors and TLC clearly anticipated as early as
September 2008 that TLC would receive the Binning House fairly immediately
after the initial transfer. No doubt TLC considered that there were benefits,
such as administrative ones, in arranging the latter transfer.

[
147
]

However, the transfer from BHPS to TLC was done by those two
societies, not by the Executors under Jessie Binning’s Will. Once the property
passed from the Executors to BHPS, the Executors no longer had any control over
the property. While there had been discussions before BHPS received the
property that it would later transfer the Binning House to TLC, BHPS could have
decided not to take the step of transferring the Binning House to TLC and the
Executors would have had no say in the matter. Once BHPS was the registered
owner of the Binning House, it was free to deal with it as it pleased, subject
to its Constitution.

[
148
]

When questioned in oral argument on how long BHPS would have had to
retain the Binning House prior to transferring it to TLC in order to be valid,
counsel for UBC replied that it would have to be more than 1/1,000 of a second
which is what it was in this case. However, this does not demonstrate that BHPS
would be required to hold the Binning House in perpetuity. There is nothing in
the Will requiring that the Entity must hold the Binning House for a certain
length of time. It can be inferred from the Will that it was not Jessie
Binning’s intention that the Entity must hold the Binning House in perpetuity
as the Will in paragraph 4(g)(iv) specifically contemplated that the Entity may
subsequently dispose of the Binning House in which case she “hoped” that the
proceeds would be paid to UBC.

[
149
]

I am persuaded by TLC’s argument that BHPS did in fact “hold,
maintain and use” the Binning House by transferring it to TLC. In effect, BHPS
held and maintained the Binning House for what is admittedly a very short
period of time; however, it used the Binning House to transfer it to TLC which
in turn has preserved the house for historical purposes in accordance with
Jessie Binning’s wish.

[
150
]

In these circumstances, I do not consider that the use of BHPS to accomplish
the
purpose
under the Will (i.e. to preserve the Binning House) falls
outside of the
scope
of the powers granted to the Executors. At the time
of the initial transfer to BHPS, BHPS had discretion and acted upon its
discretion to transfer the Binning House to TLC. Once the property passed from
the Executors to BHPS, the Executors no longer had any control over the
Binning House. This is distinguishable from
Wong
where an appointee
specifically entered into a scheme to subvert a provision in the trust
document. The contemporaneous nature of the transfers is, as I point out above,
not inconsistent with the proper exercise of the power in the first instance:
Thomas,
Goldsmid
and
Kain
.

[
151
]

Here, by analogy, it would be the act of BHPS that is really the
subject of UBC’s complaint. BHPS was given the Binning House under the terms of
the Will to “hold, maintain and use … for those
purposes it decides are desirable” (paragraph 4(g)(iii)); BHPS decided that the
purposes which it felt were desirable were to pass the Binning House on to TLC.

[
152
]

It is clear from the wording of the Will that Jessie Binning’s
intention was that the Binning House be preserved for historical purposes. The
Will states in paragraph 4(g)(iii) “if my Trustees decide
it is feasible and practical to do so, to establish a foundation or other
organization, society, association or corporation”. In this case, the Executors
did establish BHPS but no longer had any role or interest in BHPS when it
received the Binning House or when BHPS subsequently transferred the property
to TLC which then maintained it in accordance with Jessie Binning’s wishes by
preserving the property for historical purposes. I accept TLC’s submission that
“[t]here is no indication that the [Executors] had any purpose or intent to
transfer the Binning House other than to protect and preserve the property.”

[
153
]

There is no evidence of any agreement between the Executors, BHPS
and TLC to subvert the terms of the Will. Rather, the evidence demonstrates that
the Executors were concerned
about ensuring that they acted properly and that effect was given to Jessie
Binning’s intentions. Specifically, there is no
evidence of any agreement between the Executors and BHPS, let alone an
agreement that was a pre-condition to the transfer of the Binning House to BHPS,
by which the ability of BHPS to deal with the property was fettered in any way.

[
154
]

Mr. Massey’s evidence that the Binning
House was transferred to BHPS on the “understanding” that it then be
transferred to TLC is not evidence that there was an agreement or bargain in
place between the Executors and BHPS/TLC.
Black’s Law Dictionary
, 9th
ed. provides a definition of “understanding”:

1.
The process of comprehending; the act of a person who understands
something.
2.
One’s personal interpretation of an event or occurrence.
3.

An agreement, esp. of an implied or tacit nature.

[
155
]

There is no evidence that would support that Mr. Massey’s use
of the word “understanding” establishes an agreement of the sort that is
required. Rather, the use of the word in this context could equally refer to Mr. Massey’s
personal interpretation of what would happen with the Binning House. Based on
the evidence as a whole, the latter interpretation is more plausible and I find
that Mr. Massey’s interpretation or general understanding was that the
Binning House would be later transferred from BHPS to TLC. This is consistent
with the legal advice that the Executors received and their intentions.

[
156
]

Thomas’ second category is the more general one as to whether the Executors’ purpose and intention was
“foreign” in the sense that it was exercised to benefit TLC as a non-object of
the power.

[
157
]

I turn to whether TLC was an “object” under Jessie Binning’s will.
Her overriding intention is clear in paragraph 4(g)(ii) of her Will, namely
that the Binning House be preserved for historical purposes. It occurs to me
that UBC may be looking at the “objects” in this case through a mistaken lens.
Here, similar to the law of trusts, as will be discussed in the next section of
these reasons, the “object” that Jessie Binning had in mind was arguably a
charitable
purpose
, not a specific individual or entity as an “object”. The object in
this case was preservation of the Binning House. TLC had a mandate which fit
with Jessie Binning’s wish. As such, the Executors rightfully found that TLC’s management of the Binning House was
fully in keeping with that wish. The wrinkle for the Executors
was found in paragraph 4(g)(iii) of the Will which
states that the Executors must
“establish” an Entity if they wished to transfer the Binning House. The Executors were aware of this provision and

a)

particular sought legal advice as to the scope of their powers under the Will;

b)

an interpretation of the Will is such that Jessie Binning’s wish was
to preserve the Binning House and the Executors were granted significant
discretion or power to take steps to fulfill that purpose;

c)

expressly authorized under the Will;

d)

bargain between the Executors, BHPS and/or TLC as to any further dealings with

a)

A trust has two essential features: (a) it reflects a fiduciary
relationship between trustee and beneficiary in relation to property and (b) it
involves dual ownership of property by the trustee and beneficiary, with the
trustee having no beneficial ownership. As a result of the latter, the trust
property is not available to the creditors of the trustee:
Waters
at 13;

b)

A trust must provide evidence of three essential characteristics
otherwise known as the “three certainties”: certainty of intention; certainty

Waters
at
132;

c)

Certainty of subject matter is not in dispute in this case given the
characteristics and discrete nature of the Binning House; in particular this is

to be a “discrete purpose charitable property”. However, certainty of intention
and certainty of objects are in issue;

d)

With respect to certainty of intention, the language of the alleged
settlor must be imperative, rather than precatory (indicating a wish or
imposing a moral obligation, for example). There is no need for specific words to
establish the intention. While one will usually see the words “in trust” or “as
trustee for”, they are not absolutely required. However, the words used must
show that the transferee is to take on trust; if the intention is simply to
make a gift by way of a handing over the property, no trust can be established:

Waters
at 132-35;
Canada Trust Co. v. Roman Catholic Archiepiscopal
Corp. of Winnipeg
(1957),
1957 CanLII 255 (BC CA)
, 26 W.W.R. 69 (B.C.C.A.);

“charitable purpose trust” comes into existence:
Rowland
(BCSC) at paras. 68-73;

Rowland
(BCCA) at paras. 54-55. In that event, the property is held
for use only for the charitable purposes:
Rowland
(BCSC) at paras. 118-19.
A  trust for purposes is void unless the purpose is charitable:
Waters

at 163, 625;

charity or for a specific or restricted purpose, so as to be a “specific charitable

(BCSC) at para. 74;

although the court will generally lean in favour of a charitable
trust, no such approach in favour of finding a specific charitable purpose

at 188; and

at para.
21
