its preservation into the future for the public. Critical in that regard are
the following facts:

a)

it was Jessie Binning’s wish, conveyed to the Executors in the Will,
that the Binning House be preserved for historical purposes, if possible;

b)

the Executors intended to fulfill Ms. Binning’s wish by
donating the Binning House to a society for the specific purpose of preserving
the Binning House; and

c)

in accordance with BHPS’ Constitution, its first stated purpose is
to “restore, develop and preserve [the Binning House] for historical purposes …
with a view to educate and to commemorate the site”. That same language was
tracked word for word into the Deed of Gift and therefore is indicative of BHPS’s
intention in its transfer of the Binning House.

[
195
]

TLC argues that there is no language of exclusivity or exclusion
regarding the uses of or purposes of holding the Binning House. It says that
the lack of exclusive or exclusionary language in the Deed of Gift thus
militates against a finding of an intention to create a specific purpose trust
in common law and under the
CPPA
. While I agree that “historical
purposes” is a fairly generic term, in my view, it is informed by the further
references to education and the public, purposes which again were consistent
with Jessie Binning’s wish to preserve the site for future generations to come
given its historical significance. In those circumstances, BHPS could only have
been intending to preserve the site as the special place it was in terms of its
connection to B.C. Binning and its representation of his significant
contribution to modern art and architecture.

[
196
]

TLC’s general purposes are said to accord with an intention to
preserve and protect its properties, including the Binning House, in perpetuity
for so long as such intention furthers the purposes of TLC as a whole. Indeed,
it is clear that TLC’s Constitution also refers to “preservation” of “cultural”
land as part of its charitable endeavours.

[
197
]

Nonetheless, again this Deed of Trust must be considered in the
context of the actual circumstances here. The Executors sought out TLC to take
on preservation of the Binning House solely for the purpose of preserving it
into the future. The evidence of Mr. Massey and the former TLC employee affiants
must be viewed with some skepticism given the circumstances, however, what they
say rings true to some extent; namely, that the Executors would never have exercised
their discretion in setting up BHPS if they did not think that BHPS, or some
transferee such as TLC, were not taking on the task of preserving the Binning
House for that purpose. While TLC was able to generally deal with the Binning
House, it is clear that the TLC employees thought that they would be looking
after this valuable asset in perpetuity, similar to other properties owned by
TLC. To that extent, BHPS’s specific intentions were coextensive with TLC’s
general objectives but not subsumed within them.

[
198
]

I dare say that the TLC employees likely had that general intention
in relation to most of the properties TLC acquired and no doubt only recent
unfortunate circumstances have required some review of that intention. This is very
much evident from TLC’s own slogan “Special Places.
Forever
, for
Everyone” [emphasis added].

[
199
]

TLC refers to its own internal practices concerning the Binning
House. No separate accounting system was maintained for the property and
financial matters relating to the Binning House have been managed with TLC’s
other properties generally. It is apparent though that donations and expenses
relating to Binning House were coded and tracked separately. In my view, this
is not necessarily inconsistent with the “separate administration” requirement under
the
CPPA
, s. 2(1)(c)(i). This provision is more likely directed at
management of funds, as opposed to land, which might become comingled with
others held by a trustee. In this case, there is no doubt that the Binning
House itself is a discrete asset and as stated, even TLC concedes that separate
operating budgets were maintained for it.

[
200
]

TLC’s financial statements are also not determinative. In some
cases, TLC received and in fact continues to receive “restricted contributions”
or “restricted funds” which specify how funds are to be used. Those are noted
in TLC’s financial statements. In addition, at least one donation of units in a
hedge fund is referred to as being in “in trust” in which case, TLC does not
hold beneficial ownership. Binning House is not referenced specifically in the
financial statements. That treatment is not, however, conclusive.

[
201
]

Finally, TLC argues that the TLC Board was not apprised of, and
never approved, any restrictions on its acceptance of the donation. I reject
this submission as the reports by various TLC employees to the Board clearly
set out the basis upon which the Executors wished to handle the preservation of
the Binning House. Further, the execution of the Deed of Gift was executed by
two TLC Board members and is further support for the conclusion that the TLC
Board was fully aware of the specific purpose of the gift. Again, it is the
Deed of Gift and the overall circumstances which support a finding of intention
on the part of BHPS to transfer the Binning House on a specific purpose trust.
That same document and those same circumstances amply support that TLC intended
to accept the Binning House on that basis.

[
202
]

I conclude that BHPS intended to transfer the Binning House to TLC
not for TLC’s general
charitable purposes, but pursuant to a specific purpose trust so as to preserve
it for generations to come. In addition, I conclude that the requirement under the

CPPA
, s. 2(1)(c) is met in that it has been shown “by necessary
implication” that BHPS’ intention was that the Binning House would be kept and
administered separately and used by TLC to advance the specified charitable
purpose with respect to determining that it is “discrete purpose charitable
property”.

(D)      Is the
Specific Purpose Trust a Sham?

[
203
]

In the alternative, TLC takes the position that if the Deed of Trust
created a specific purpose trust in relation to the Binning House, and as such
created a restriction on TLC’s ownership of the Binning House, such a restriction
is a legal “sham” and therefore, void.

[
204
]

The oft quoted test for determining whether there is a “sham”
transaction is found in the comments of Lord Diplock in
Snook v. London and
West Riding Investments Ltd.

[1967] 2 Q.B. 786 at 802
:

….it means acts done or documents executed
by the parties to the “sham” which are
intended
by them to give to third
parties or to the court the appearance of creating between the parties legal
rights and obligations different from the actual rights and obligations (if
any) which the parties intend to create. But one thing, I think, is clear in
legal principle, morality and the authorities … that for acts or documents to
be a “sham”, with whatever legal consequences follow from this, all the parties
thereto must have a common intention that the acts or documents are not to
create the legal rights and obligations which they give the appearance of
creating.

[Emphasis added]

[
205
]

As can be seen from the above statement, the essence of a sham
transaction arises from the intention of
all parties
to the instrument.
As stated in
Waters
at 146, this concept is different than the
requirement of certainty of intention and is more concerned with the intention
of the settlor to perpetrate an “illegality” or “illusory trust”, as a result
of which the trust is void.

[
206
]

This principle from
Snook
has been applied in Canada generally:

Minister of National Revenue v. Cameron
,
1972 CanLII 188 (SCC)
, [1974] S.C.R. 1062 at 1068;
Trident
Foreshore Lands Ltd. v. Brown
,
2004 BCSC 1365
at para.
39
.

[
207
]

In addition, the principle has been applied in Canada in respect of alleged
“sham trusts”, often in cases involving bankruptcies and fraudulent
transactions affecting creditors. In
Hirji v. Scavetta
(1993),
1993 CanLII 5452 (ON CTGD)
, 15 O.R.
(3d) 371, [1993] O.J. No. 2546 (Gen. Div.) at para.
32
, the court
found that a transfer in trust was designed to avoid creditors. In
Biggar
(Re)
,
2005 BCSC 1657
, the court, after reviewing other examples of “sham
trust” (para. 23), concluded that the bankrupt had dealt with the subject
property as his alone and had never intended to divest any beneficial interest
in the shares.

[
208
]

In
Forsyth (Re)
,
2010 BCSC 1720
, and following
Biggar

and
Hirji
, the court found a declaration of trust to be void as an
attempt by a bankrupt to shield his assets from his creditors. At para. 24,
the court accepted that post “trust” conduct was relevant to a consideration
and determination of the true intention of the settlor.

[
209
]

TLC argues that various circumstances here point to the fact that it
was never intended by both BHPS and TLC that there would be restrictions on
TLC’s use of or rights to the Binning House.

[
210
]

It is clear that the signatories to the Deed of Gift (Mr. Turner
and Ms. Baker) were both employees of TLC and members/directors/officers
of BHPS. Firstly, TLC argues that they both signed a Form A Freehold Transfer
evidencing a transfer of the Binning House from BHPS to TLC and that is true;
however, it is equally true that they also required, as part of the overall
transaction strategy, that this separate Deed of Gift be signed. As noted
above, if the true intention was not to impose any specific trust conditions,
then rhetorically, why was this instrument required at all?

[
211
]

Secondly, TLC argues that both Mr. Turner and Ms. Baker
have only now recently asserted their positions as current or former board
members of BHPS to derail TLC’s reorganization efforts. I would reiterate my
comments above in that while there may be some skepticism on this point, their
positions are consistent with the actions of all persons involved in the
transfer from BHPS to TLC.

[
212
]

Thirdly, TLC argues that despite Ms. Baker’s present position,
she authored a report to the TLC Board recommending accepting the donation of
the Binning House with no mention of any restrictions. While that may be the
case, the report from September 2008 cannot be taken as a definitive statement
as to the terms upon which the transfer was to take place. Needless to say, the
fact that the Deed of Trust was later prepared and signed on behalf of both
BHPS and TLC also indicates that other terms were later discussed and agreed
upon.

[
213
]

Fourthly, TLC argues that Mr. Turner and Ms. Baker would
have known at the time the Deed of Gift was executed that TLC would treat the
Binning House in the same manner as all TLC’s properties. This argument is
largely centered on the manner in which the accounting of revenue and expenses
relating to the Binning House took place. When TLC received donations intended
by the donor to be applied to any given property, these donations were
deposited into TLC’s general account and applied, as needed, to any property or
to TLC’s general needs, irrespective of the donor’s intent. In most cases, the
costs related to a property exceed the donations or other revenues related to
such property. Additional general revenue was therefore used to fund TLC’s
properties.

[
214
]

Revenue from donations and other receipts for the Binning House were
received by TLC and deposited in its general account. Disbursements in respect
of the Binning House were paid out of the general account as needed and were
not restricted to the revenue received specifically for the Binning House. TLC did
not administer a separate bank account for the management of the Binning House.

[
215
]

In my view, the manner in which these revenue and expenses were
accounted for is hardly determinative of the issue in relation to the legal
designation of the subject matter of the trust - i.e. the Binning House. As I
have said, revenue and expenses relating to the property were separately coded
so that TLC was able to quickly determine the financial operating status of the
asset. But that is quite a separate matter as to whether the asset itself, as
opposed perhaps to income derived from it, is held in trust. The same can be
said as to the basis upon which expenses were handled.

[
216
]

Fifthly, TLC argues that Mr. Turner and Ms. Baker
would have known that the TLC Board was not bound by the wishes of any donor.
The TLC Bylaws provide:

18.05   The
Board of Directors is not bound by the wishes of any donor if such wishes are,
at the time of the gift or at a future time, inimical to the purposes of [TLC]
…

Despite this provision, I fail to see how
this allows the TLC Board to simply ignore a legal trust obligation, rather
than simply a “wish”, imposed at the time of transfer. Bylaw 18.03 provides
that TLC “may refuse to accept any donations, contributions, gifts, or bequests
of any kind whatsoever at the sole discretion of the Board of Directors”. In
this case, I am satisfied that the TLC was well aware as to the basis upon
which the Binning House was being transferred, per the Deed of Gift. As such,
the Board agreed to accept the donation on that basis.

[
217
]

Sixthly, TLC argues that Mr. Turner and Ms. Baker would
have been aware of the ability to restrict TLC’s use of donated property
through Bylaw 20, by which the Board could declare certain properties “inalienable”.
TLC further says that there is no evidence that this option was discussed at
the time of the transfer to TLC as a condition of the transfer. I see no merit
in this argument for two reasons: firstly, this mechanism is one available to
the Board
after
a donation is made - a self-imposed restriction as it
were; and secondly, in my view it is likely that the Board saw no need to do
this in relation to Binning House by reason of the Deed of Gift.

[
218
]

The simple question here is - did BHPS and TLC intend that the Deed
of Gift having the meaning which it conveyed? In my view, nothing in TLC’s
post-Deed of Gift conduct is indicative of any contrary intent nor is it
indicative of any “sham”. I find as a fact that the intention of BHPS and TLC
in executing the Deed of Gift was to reflect exactly what is stated in that
document; namely, that TLC was to receive Binning House for the purpose of
restoring, developing and preserving the Binning House as stated.

(E)       Was There Certainty
Of Objects?

[
219
]

In terms of satisfying the requirement of certainty of objects, both
the common law and the
CPPA
(
s. 1
, definition of “charitable purpose”)
require that there be a purpose recognized at law as being charitable.

[
220
]

In the further alterative, TLC says that the purposes set out in the
Deed of Gift, namely “restoring, developing and preserving the Binning House …
for historical purposes with a view to educating the public and commemorating
the site”, are not purposes recognized as “charitable” at law. Accordingly, TLC
says there is no special purpose trust relating to the Binning House and that
the gift comprised the full legal and beneficial title for TLC’s general
societal purposes.

[
221
]

A charitable purpose must benefit the public:
Waters

at 679;
Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. Canada
(Minister of National Revenue)
,
1999 CanLII 704 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 10 at paras.
41
, 45-51,
148. In
Vancouver Society
, Gonthier J. for the minority further
clarified that there are two components to a public benefit:

[41]      … [t]here must be an objectively
measurable and socially useful
benefit
conferred; and it must be a benefit
available to a sufficiently large section of the population to be considered a public
benefit.

[Emphasis in
original]

[
222
]

In
Vancouver Society
, the entire court (majority of the court
at para. 144) adopted the classification of four purposes recognized as
charitable at common law in
Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income Tax
v. Pemsel
,
1891 CanLII 21 (FOREP)
, [1891] A.C. 531 (U.K.H.L.), as follows:

a)

the relief of poverty;

b)

the advancement of education;

c)

the advancement of religion;

d)

for other purposes beneficial to the community,
not falling under the preceding heads.

[
223
]

As the court in
Vancouver Society
cautioned, one must be
careful to distinguish between charitable
purposes
and charitable
activities
.
Looking at the Deed of Gift, it can be seen that the purposes are “historical
purposes with a view to educating the public and commemorating the site” and in
part, the activities by which those purposes are obtained are by “restoring,
developing and preserving the Binning House”.

[
224
]

The issues are firstly, whether such purposes come within the second
category of “advancement of education” and secondly, whether such purposes come
within the fourth category as “beneficial to the community”, so as to constitute
a charitable purpose at law.

[
225
]

Dealing with the first issue, the majority in
Vancouver
Society
adopts a more inclusive approach to education for the purpose of charity
law than had previously been applied by Canadian courts to include “informal
training initiatives, aimed at teaching necessary life skills or providing
information toward a practical end, so long as these are truly geared at the
training of the mind and not just the promotion of a particular point of view”:
para. 168. Both the majority (paras. 168-71) and the minority (para. 78)
were cautious in circumscribing what activities come within this category. The
whole court agreed that the “information or training is provided in a
structured manner and for a genuinely educational purpose -- this is, to
advance the knowledge or abilities of the recipients” (paras. 77, 169).
Further, for the majority, Iacobucci J. stated:

[171]    … the
threshold criterion for an educational activity must be some legitimate,
targeted attempt at educating others, whether through formal or informal
instruction, training, plans of self-study, or otherwise. Simply providing an
opportunity for people to educate themselves, such as by making available
materials with which this might be accomplished but need not be, is not enough.

[
226
]

In
Vancouver Society
, the purpose of “educat[ing] members of
the Community at large, including immigrant & visible minority women, on
the needs and concerns of immigrant & visible minority women in Canada” was
found to be a charitable purpose because of the commitment of the Society to “provide
educational forums, classes, workshops and seminars” to enable its constituents
to obtain employment. However, consistent with the views of the minority above,
the majority in
Vancouver Society
noted that, in the context of
education, the class must be substantial, and the benefits cannot be provided
exclusively to a class of private individuals defined only by their relationship
to the organization (paras. 4, 174).

[
227
]

Even from TLC’s point of view, there is no
dispute that the Binning House was to be used for educational purposes. In its
grant application from October 2010, TLC stated:

When TLC manages
any particular site, we ensure that the site is accessible to the public by
providing educational and recreational activities. TLC plans to use the B.C.
Binning site to inspire and educate artists, architects, school children and
other interested members of the West Vancouver community. …

[
228
]

TLC also prepared a Conservation Plan for the Binning House in March
2012. In that document, TLC outlines its vision to preserve and manage “in
perpetuity” the Binning House “as a cultural icon and asset relating to the
West Coast Modernism movement”. Consistent with its objectives, TLC, apparently
mostly through the
ad hoc
community group known as the “Binning House
Advisory Committee”, arranged for various public events at the Binning House
including tours, social events, photo shoots, discussion groups and children’s
camps, all with a focus on art, design and architecture. In accordance with the
Conservation Plan, TLC also indicated an intention to increase public use and
programming through lectures, workshops, exhibitions and further tours.

[
229
]

The AG submits and I agree that the purpose in accordance with the
Deed of Gift is to preserve Binning House for historical purposes and to
educate the public about the architecture of that era and B.C. Binning’s very
important contribution to the birth of the West Coast modern architecture by
his creation of the Binning House.

[
230
]

I was not referred by any counsel to any authorities where the
preservation of a structure such as a house for such a purpose has been found
to be a “charitable purpose”. However, the reasoning in
Re Pinion
,

[1964] 2 W.L.R. 919 (C.A.)
is instructive. In that case, the testator had
gifted his studio and its contents with the intention that it be open to the
public as a museum. The issue arose as to whether the bequest was a valid
charitable trust. The Court of Appeal did not disagree with the proposition
that such a gift might constitute a charitable purpose in appropriate
circumstances. However, the court resoundingly found that the objects comprised
in this gift would do nothing to advance education in aesthetics or history.
Harman L.J. was even more direct in stating at 928 that “no useful object
[would] be served in foisting upon the public this mass of junk”.

[
231
]

Even before
Vancouver Society
,
Montgomery J. adopted an expansive view of “education” sufficient for
charitable purposes in
Shapiro (Re)
(1979),
1979 CanLII 1678 (ON HCJ)
, 27 O.R. (2d) 517 (H. Ct. J.).
The court quoted Justice Vaisey in
Re Shaw’s Will Trusts
,
[1952] Ch.
163
, as follows:

… I think
“education” includes … not only teaching, but the promotion or encouragement of
these arts and graces of life which are, after all, perhaps the finest and best
part of the human character (
Shapiro (Re)

at 519).

[
232
]

Of course, no one here has suggested that the Binning House and its
contents are “junk”. To the contrary, everyone, including TLC, acknowledges the
significance of the property. It is inherently significant from an
architectural point of view in terms of its design elements. Even beyond those
elements, B.C. Binning’s art is an integral part of the property. It is for these
reasons, and no doubt others, that TLC described the Binning House as a
“spectacular mix between art and architecture, among the first of its kind in
Canada”.

[
233
]

In the above circumstances, I have no hesitation in finding that the
preservation of the Binning House for the purposes set out in the Deed of Gift
comes within the purview of a “charitable purpose” relating to the advancement
of education.

[
234
]

Given my conclusion above, it is not necessary
to consider whether the purposes under the Deed of Gift come within the fourth
category in
Pemsel
, namely another “purpose beneficial to the community
not falling under the preceding heads”. As stated by
Waters
, at 720,
this encompasses purposes which are diverse in nature, where no particular
purpose is dominant. Nevertheless, I will address this issue briefly.

[
235
]

As stated by
Waters
at 721:

…while each of
the purposes in this miscellaneous class must be for the benefit of the public
at large, or an appreciable section of the public, the purpose itself must have
a nature or quality which conforms to the notion of charity derived from the 1601
Act.

[
236
]

In other words, the purpose must be beneficial in a way that trust law
regards as “charitable”. As the court noted in
Vancouver Society
, the
requirement that the purpose benefit in a way the law regards as charitable is
circular and not particularly helpful in determining what falls within this
category (paras. 45, 177). Iacobucci J. adopted what he concluded was a
useful approach from
D'Aguiar v. Guyana Commissioner of Inland Revenue
, [1970] T.R. 31
(P.C.) at 33:

[The Court] must
first consider the trend of those decisions which have established certain
objects as charitable under this heading, and ask whether, by reasonable
extension or analogy, the instant case may be considered to be in line with
these. Secondly, it must examine certain accepted anomalies to see whether they
fairly cover the objects under consideration. Thirdly -- and this is really a
cross-check upon the others -- it must ask whether, consistently with the
objects declared, the income and property in question can be applied for
purposes clearly falling outside the scope of charity: if so, the argument for
charity must fail (
Vancouver Society
at para. 46).

[
237
]

Accordingly, courts have built upon the traditional heads of charity
by way of “analogy upon analogy”:
Waters
at 731.

[
238
]

TLC argues that “historical purposes” or “commemoration of a site”
are vague concepts and their recognition as a specific charitable purpose that
restricts TLC’s rights to and dealings with the Binning House would go beyond
“analogy upon analogy” with recognized charitable purposes. With respect
though, these phrases are taken out of context and are not “stand alone”
purposes in accordance with the Deed of Gift. Rather, they inform the overall
purpose in the document which is stated to be preservation of the Binning House
for the purposes of education of the public in terms of architecture and art.

[
239
]

In
Save the Heritage Simpson Covenant Society
,
the court found that a transfer of land for “municipal purposes” was sufficient
to constitute a charitable purpose:

[120]

B
y
its ordinary
meaning “municipal purposes” connotes the use of property for such things as a
public library, a police station, a city hall, an arena, a convention centre,
and a public museum or art gallery. All of these purposes, in my view, could be
considered as charitable in nature. Any of these facilities promotes the
welfare and wellbeing of the community as much as park land or a show ground.
In the British text,
Tudor on Charities
, 6
th
ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1967) at
pp. 85 to 87, the authors note that trusts for achieving objects of
general public utility such as museums, libraries, public halls, reading rooms
and an observatory, to which the general public have access as of right, have
all been held to be charitable purposes. In my view, if characterizing
the Simpson Covenants as describing a charitable purpose is regarded as a
development of the law defining charitable purpose, I find it is only a
permissible, incremental change and not a large step requiring legislative
approval.

[
240
]

I see no difference between a charitable purpose in setting up a
museum to house historical objects as opposed to one setting up Binning House
which itself is an historical object, as discussed above.

[
241
]

TLC argues further that preservation of heritage-designated properties
as a charitable purpose at law could have significant and far-reaching
implications for numerous private individuals or organizations who own
heritage-designated properties, both in terms of tax status and beneficial
ownership. I do not, however, see any merit to this “slippery slope” argument.
Not every old house and efforts to preserve that old house will attract
consideration of these concepts. Many people in a variety of contexts take
particular care to preserve heritage houses. But true charitable purposes will,
as discussed above, depend on intentions to benefit the public and the nature
of the charitable purpose.

[
242
]

I conclude that the purposes set out in the Deed of Gift are
charitable within the meaning of the fourth category from
Pemsel
as a
purpose “beneficial to the community”.

[
243
]

It is somewhat odd that TLC’s own activities are in direct conflict
with its submissions in this regard. TLC has three other properties - Ross Bay
Villa, Abkhazi Garden and the Keating Farm Estate -
which all involve TLC’s efforts to preserve various heritage buildings on
Vancouver Island. TLC no doubt would argue that its purpose in maintaining
these properties is in accordance with its overall “charitable” purposes. As
with these properties, the preservation of the Binning House can be considered as
coming within TLC’s general charitable purpose per para. 2(a) of its
Constitution by “improv[ing] the education, health and welfare of the general
public and to benefit the community as a whole by the … preservation … of …
areas of … historical, cultural, … value”.

[
244
]

On a final note, as the AG points out, even if one could conclude
that some aspects of the purposes under the Deed of Gift were “non-charitable”
in nature, if a charitable purpose is linked conjunctively or disjunctively
with a non-charitable purpose, the gift, devise or bequest is not invalid but
operates only for the benefit of the charitable purpose:
Law and Equity Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996 c. 253, s. 47.

(F)       Did the
Trust Cease to Apply?

[
245
]

TLC next argues that even if a specific purpose trust was imposed at
the time BHPS transferred the Binning House TLC, the trust ceased to apply in
accordance with the
CPPA
as the Binning House was not utilized by TLC to
further the specific purpose.

[
246
]

TLC refers to the provisions in
s. 2(1)
of
the
CPPA
which provide that property is discrete
purpose charitable property “
if and for so long as
that property is
kept, administered and used in accordance with the intention [of the donor in

s. 2(1)
(c)]” [emphasis added], namely, keeping the property separate from
other property and using the property exclusively to advance the specified
charitable purpose. Further, provisions in the
CPPA
which track this
same language include:

3
1)      Property that is discrete purpose charitable property
retains its character as discrete purpose charitable property
if and for so
long as the property is kept, administered and used

(a)  in accordance
with the intention of the donor of the property referred to in section 2 (1)
(c) or, if the court has made an order in respect of the property under
subsection (4) of this section or under section 4 (1) (b), in accordance with
the intention expressed in that order, and

(b)  without
limiting paragraph (a) of this subsection, exclusively for the advancement of
the discrete purpose.

[Emphasis

[

TLC contends that the legislation must be
interpreted on the presumption that the legislature intended to avoid

Sullivan on the

and
Rowland

… designed to ensure that money or other

… The purpose of this act is to allow a

The act is also intended to establish a fair
balance

between the interests of donors and charitable organizations on

Hansard
37th Parl., 5th Sess., Vol. 26 No. 9 (18 October 2004) at

Hansard
37th Parl., 5th Sess., Vol. 26 No. 12 (20 October

Rowland

[
251

Further, the manner in which the accounting relating to the Binning

required.

[
252

It is not necessary to decide what circumstances may come within the

and if so, whether

[
253
]

However, reading the

as a whole, I can see no

the legislative intent found in the
CPPA
, which

seeks to ensure
that gifts are used for the specified charitable purposes.

[

In any event, the
CPPA
, s. 5 clearly
and expressly provides that nothing in that
Act
limits or affects the

applies. On
this issue, the
CPPA
provisions simply add to the already existing
common law relating to trusts, rather than detracting from it. As
Waters

observes at 14, it is no defence by a trustee that he or she has failed to
abide by the terms of the trust: “…it is vital to observe that the trust
beneficiary’s interest continues to adhere in the trust property despite
wrongful conversion or alienation by the trustee.”

[
255
]

I agree with the AG that it would anomalous to consider that a
trustee could escape its statutory obligations under the

or its common

CPPA

nor the common law relating to trusts supports TLC’s argument in this respect.

(ii)        If the Binning House is subject to a statutory or common
law trust in the hands of TLC, should the trust be modified?

[
256
]

In the alternative, TLC argues that if the Binning House remains
subject to a specific purpose trust, the trust fails due to the subsequent or intervening

does not argue that the carrying out of the charitable purpose in relation to
the Binning House was initially impossible or impracticable and events
subsequent to the transfer to TLC in 2008 would appear to confirm that. However,

allow TLC to use the Binning House for its general purposes, as that is
cy-près

or “close to” the original intention.

[
257
]

Tudor
describes
the principle of carrying a charitable intention into effect by means of
cy-près

as follows (at 215, 217):

It is a fundamental principle of the law of
charities which has been established for centuries that wherever a clear
intention to devote property to charity is shown, and that intention is not
confined to a particular form of charity which is initially impracticable, or a
purpose which is illegal, effect must be given to it. The law distinguishes
between the charitable intention and the mode of executing it. The particular
mode of application indicated by the donor is not considered to be of the
essence of the gift, and the law makes provision for the charitable intention
to be carried into effect
cy-près
, that is to say, by substituting for
the mode indicated by the donor another mode as similar as possible to the mode
indicated.

….

Where a gift is liable to fail it will only
be saved by the court if the objects of the gift are exclusively charitable and
if the subject-matter of the gift is certain and validly assured. Further, the
property would only be applied
cy-près
, that is, for purposes as nearly
as possible to the purposes which have failed,
if the purpose in question
had become impossible or impracticable to perform. Formerly, “impossibility”
and “impracticability” were narrowly defined: inexpediency or uneconomic
circumstances were not sufficient
.

[Emphasis added].

[
258
]

The courts have not
given a definition of “impossibility” or “impracticability”. However,
Waters

at 774 states what “impossibility” is not:

Impossibility
does not mean that the trust cannot be carried into effect without the
assistance of the court. It refers in most instances to situations where events
have taken place between the writing of the instrument of gift and the
instrument taking effect which prevent the object of the trust from being
carried out at all.

At 775, with respect to
“impracticability”,
Waters
refers to various authorities where the
objects were held to be so, “in the sense that, though they still could be
carried out, the whole intention of the donor has really been overtaken by
events …”.

[
259
]

Further,
Waters
, similar to
Tudor

above, states at 777 that the requirement of impossibility and impracticability
and the narrow circumstances in which such they can arise remain important:

… the courts have refused to approve
cy-près

schemes which are based on the argument that the proposed objects better
provide for contemporary needs than the objects the donor chose. Even if there
is a general charitable intent which would continue to be furthered by proposed
objects as well as by the original objects, English courts have taken the view
that as long as the original objects can still be carried out, even if with
more limited value than they once would have had, they cannot be interfered
with.
That is to say, impossibility and impracticability have been kept
within narrow limits, a restriction which has had particular significance in
the handling of
cy-près
applications on the basis of supervening impossibility
and impracticability
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[

]

In addition to the common law, the

also sets out the court’s authority to impose a
cy-près
or “consistent” scheme
in
s. 3(3)
and
3(4)
:

(3)        Unless this Act provides
otherwise, the court may make, in relation to discrete purpose charitable
property and a charity holding discrete purpose charitable property, any order
it may make in relation to any charitable trust property and any charity
holding charitable trust property.

(4)        Without limiting subsection (3),
if a charity holding discrete purpose charitable property is unwilling or
unable to continue to keep, administer and use the property to advance the
discrete purpose, the court may make whatever orders, including arrangements,
it considers appropriate, including transferring the property to a new charity,
so that the property is kept, administered and used to

(a)        advance
the discrete purpose, or

(b)        advance another charitable
purpose that the court considers is consistent with the discrete purpose.

[
261
]

In support of its argument, TLC relies upon
Lee v. North
Vancouver School District No. 44
,
2011 BCSC 222
, which appears to be
the only case which has, to date, considered and applied the

.

In
Lee
, the trustee School Board sought to be relieved of its
obligations in relation to a certain trust because it was no longer willing to
continue to keep, administer and use the funds for the specific charitable

CPPA
or alternatively, by
application of the court’s
cy-pr
è
s
jurisdiction. The court
applied its broad jurisdiction to grant an “appropriate” order under
s. 3(4)

of the

in substituting a trustee for the Board where the Board was
“unwilling” to continue. In addition, a variation of the trust in the hands of
the new trustee (the Foundation) was necessary given the impracticability of
performance of the terms of the original trust in the future: paras. 52-68.
In the alternative, the court found that relief was also available under its
cy-près

jurisdiction. The court varied the terms of the trust because the trustee had
established intervening “economic impracticability of the continuation of
adherence to the strict terms of the Trust verging upon impossibility”: para. 73.

[
263
]

Central to the court’s decision on both fronts was that, despite
allowing time to the parties to do so, no substitute trustee had been found to
undertake the duties of the trustee under the Trust in accordance with its
terms; only the new trustee, the Foundation, had come forward but it was
unwilling to take it on such terms. In addition, in order to accommodate any
other “white knight” trustee that might come forward to operate the trust as
intended, the court stayed execution of the order for 60 days to find a
substitute trustee: para. 80. Of significance was that the court in
Lee

granted the relief with the overriding intention to “… continue to advance the
charitable purposes of the Trust
to the greatest extent now possible
(para. 74)
[Emphasis added].

[

The orders granted in
Lee
included transferring the trust fund
to the Foundation on the condition that it would establish a scholarship fund

Lee
at para.
68
).

The AG refers to two authorities. In
Bentley v. Anglican Synod of
the Diocese of New Westminster
,
2010 BCCA 506
, the court considered the
issue as to whether the trial judge should have rejected a

order
in the main action and applied such an order in the “Chun action”. I do not

[

Of more assistance is
Roman Catholic Bishop
of Bathurst v. New Brunswick
,
2010 NBQB 400
. Similar to the comments of
Waters

and
Tudor
, the court stressed that the
cy-près
doctrine can only
be applied in limited circumstances:

[46]      With that context in mind, it is
reasonable to expect that a judge would not lightly interfere with the original
intention of the settlors, those persons who created these trusts, as, at the
time each was created, it was their intention that the money bequeathed or
transferred by donation be used for the specific purpose set out in the trust
document in perpetuity.

[47]

It must be firmly born in mind when considering the application of “a

cy-près
scheme” that the public must continue to have confidence that
when a charitable bequest or grant is made it will only be in limited and
justifiable circumstances that a court will step in and alter what was intended
by the person who created the trust. To do otherwise would threaten and likely
damage the confidence the public have in the enduring nature of any charitable
trust that might be contemplated for creation in the future.

[48]

For that reason, the law does not allow a judge to alter the
specific objects of a trust except in such narrow circumstances. Those
circumstances are limited to situations in which the specific objects of the
trust are impossible to achieve, are illegal or are or have become
impracticable. It is in those circumstances that the doctrine of
cy-près
can
be applied to remedy the difficulties arising from the implementation of or
continued accomplishment of the specific objects of the trust.

[

]

In

, the court was faced with the opposite problem of

was made under
cy-près
to allow the Diocese access to a certain portion

]

(Ont.

cy-près
at para. 72. The

a)

the court found that while the donors or settlors referred to the

mission in perpetuity, which was significantly advanced by allowing the

b)

only
surplus

and

, para. 76(6)).

[

272
]

were considered in both

and

.

upon which TLC can

at 375, “[a] charitable gift will not fail
for want of a trustee”.

and
Bathurst

, s. 3(4)

is of general application and provides a

cy‑près
,
then the introduction of this specific provision was unnecessary:
CPPA
,
ss. 3(3),
5
.

s. 3(4)
of the

CPPA
, s. 3(4). Section 3(4) of the

[
282
]

The relief which may be granted by the court
may
include, but
may not necessarily include, a transfer of the property to a “new charity”. Whether

a)

advance the “discrete purpose”; or

b)

advance another “charitable purpose”.

]

With respect to the second option, the court has discretion to modify

i.          firstly, the other “charitable purpose” must be one recognized
from
Pemsel
as discussed above, which may include the payment of debts
or liabilities, including expenses, arising from the actual, intended or
purported advancement of that purpose (see
CPPA
, s. 1, definition

CPPA
, s. 1, definition of “discrete
purpose (b)”); and

“consistent with” the discrete purpose.

]

of the

. It must be noted, however,

the Binning House, if possible, as discussed above. In particular, it cannot be
determined whether someone else will take over to advance the discrete purpose
of preserving Binning House into the future.

[
292
]

If there is no such person, or if someone is only willing to accept
the trust on a modified basis, those would be very relevant considerations for
the court to consider. In that respect, I will repeat again that no one, save
for Mr. Wall, has yet stepped forward to take over the Binning House, with
that person having the financial wherewithal to finance the substantial
monetary obligations for structural repairs and ongoing maintenance for the
Binning House in perpetuity. Good intentions are one thing, but they must, at
least in this case, be married to a cheque book.

[
293
]

If TLC is not able to sell the Binning House on trust and no one
else emerges, then what is to become of the Binning House? The generosity of
the District in granting tax exemptions might continue but no doubt other
ongoing operational costs must be paid for, as with any old house. Is the court
to require that TLC pay these costs and if so, on what basis and with what and
whose money? If these costs are not incurred, then this cultural gem will be
endangered perhaps beyond repair, despite the heritage status and the Bylaws.

[
294
]

As TLC points out, if there is a specific purpose trust requiring
TLC to retain the Binning House that will, somewhat ironically, likely ensure
that the specific purpose imposed by BHPS is
not
fulfilled and that the
testamentary wishes of Jessie Binning are
not
fulfilled. Here, TLC
argues that serious damage will be incurred to both TLC and the Binning House
in these circumstances by reason of its inability to finance restoration and
maintenance of the Binning House.

[
295
]

These are all valid arguments but, as discussed above, I decline to
address them at this time on the basis of either
cy-près
or the
CPPA
,
s. 3(4) without a full evidentiary record regarding efforts of TLC to find
a substitute trustee and the practical consequences of any failure to find such
a trustee.

[
296
]

On a final note, TLC has taken the position that it is an
appropriate exercise of the Court’s inherent and
CCAA
jurisdiction to
allow the Binning House to be held by TLC in trust for its general purposes and
to authorize the sale of the Binning House through the
CCAA
process, even
in the face of trust obligations that may apply to those assets. TLC argues
that this court should exercise its broad jurisdiction under the
CCAA
,
s. 11 to “make any order that it considers appropriate in the
circumstances”.

[
297
]

As I stated earlier, no issue of paramountcy arises in this case. The
issues raised on this application are largely not matters of discretion,
whether relating to the issue of advancing the policy objectives of the
CCAA

or otherwise:
Century Services Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2010
SCC 60
at para.
70
. Rather, they are matters of determining the rights of
TLC and other stakeholders in the Binning House. As such, the issues are to be
decided based on the law that applies generally.

[
298
]

In respect of the trust issues, in my view the matters are to be
decided on the basis of the law already cited to me, whether under the
cy-près

doctrine or under the
CPPA
. In respect of either or both the
cy-près

doctrine and the
CPPA
, s. 3(4), it may be the case that any decision
or discretion to be exercised in favour of TLC will be consonant with the
policy objectives of the
CCAA
, but that remains to be seen.

[
299
]

Accordingly, in these circumstances, TLC’s application to approve the
sale to BJW is adjourned generally, with liberty to reset the application with
further evidence in respect of the potential application of either the
cy-près

doctrine or the
CPPA
, s. 3(4).

(iii)       In any event, is the Binning
House exigible by TLC’s creditors?

[
300
]

TLC submits that the Binning House is exigible to TLC’s creditors,
including the DIP Lenders, and thus it must be available to TLC to be sold so
as to facilitate a restructuring that is in part aimed at benefiting TLC’s
creditors.

[
301
]

Firstly, TLC relies on the reasoning of the Ontario Court of Appeal
in the
Christian Brothers
litigation. I have already discussed this
issue earlier in these reasons and I have referred to the opinion of Braidwood
J.A. in
Rowland
. In addition, having found that the Binning House was
given to TLC under a specific purpose trust or a “discrete purpose charitable
property” per the
CPPA
, s. 3(3) and
(4)
, the comments of the
Ontario Court of Appeal are of no assistance to TLC on this issue.

[
302
]

Secondly, TLC submits that there are additional
legislative and policy considerations when the subject matter of an alleged
trust is real property and there could be mortgagees or others who granted
credit to a debtor company on the basis of an apparent and registered legal and
beneficial title.

[
303
]

In British Columbia, land registration is
completed on the basis of the Torrens system.
Section 23
of the
Land Title
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 250 (the “
LTA
”) provides for the effect
of land registration subject to certain exceptions, none of which apply here:

23 (2)   An
indefeasible title, as long as it remains in force and uncancelled, is
conclusive evidence at law and in equity, as against the Crown and all other
persons, that the person named in the title as registered owner is indefeasibly
entitled to an estate in fee simple to the land described in the indefeasible
title ...

[
304
]

Section 23(2)
of the
LTA
provides for a statutory
presumption that registered title is conclusive evidence of the ownership of
legal and beneficial interests. However, the presumption can be rebutted in
some circumstances, such as by the operation of a resulting trust; where there
is an agreement between the parties that is contrary to the registered title; or
to take account of the underlying equitable interests between parties:
Bajwa
v. Pannu
,
2007 BCCA 260
at paras.
9-10
, 14.

[
305
]

In
Gill v. Bucholtz
,
2009 BCCA 137
, the Court considered the
presumption in
s. 23(2)
of the
LTA
in the context of a fraudulent
transfer of the property and the subsequent granting of a mortgage to a
bona
fide
lender. However, in considering that section and others in the
LTA
,
including
s. 25.1(1)
and
26
, the Court found that the
LTA
preserved
the principle of
nemo dat quod non habet
in relation to registered
interests less than fee simple, such as charges: paras. 5, 19, 21 and 26.

[
306
]

TLC refers to
Taylor Ventures Ltd. (Trustee) v. High Meadow
Holdings Ltd.
,
2006 BCSC 1095
at para.
34
, aff’d
2008 BCCA 80
, leave
to appeal to SCC refused, [2008] S.C.C.A. No. 159 as standing for the
proposition that as against a mortgagee in good faith, where no fraud on the
part of the mortgagee has been shown, a mortgagee has the ability to enforce a
loan as against property held in trust where the loan was made on the basis of
who is registered on title. However, the facts in that case were markedly
different that those here in that the transfer to the trustee was later set
aside and declared void pursuant to fraudulent conveyance legislation.

[
307
]

In my view, this argument can be disposed of on the basis that, at
all times, it was well known by the DIP Lenders that trust issues had arisen in
relation to TLC’s assets generally and would be, if necessary, decided in the
course of the restructuring proceedings.

[
308
]

The evidence before the court on the initial hearing of the petition
included:

a)         the
Affidavit of Briony Penn sworn October 4, 2013 which referred to:

i.      the identification of several properties being candidates
for immediate disposition (which did not appear to include the Binning House)
having … “no or only limited restrictions under trust law or the
CPPA
” (para. 50);
and

iii.    potential prejudice to the creditors of TLC and the entire
stakeholder group arising from “unique issues with respect to the trust
conditions attaching to its properties, and the effects of the
CPPA
” (para. 76),
and

b)         the
report dated October 4, 2013 of Wolrige Mahon Limited, as the proposed Monitor,
which stated:

i.      the
CPPA
that specified “conditions that apply to any
potential disposition or transfer of the Properties owned by TLC” (para. 2.2);

ii.     that [b]y design, the …
CPPA
hamper/prevent “TLC from
divesting itself of Properties to inappropriate parties or using them for
inappropriate purposes” (para. 3.1); and

iii.    “disposition or transfer of the Properties will be hampered
or precluded by … Restrictions on certain Properties donated to TLC on the
condition they could not be sold or transferred (specified intent of donor)” (para. 3.2.4).

[
309
]

In addition, the relief sought by TLC and the DIP Lenders and
granted in the Initial Order on October 7, 2013 also confirm that in no way was
it intended that the DIP Lenders’ Charge would obtain priority save in respect
of TLC’s beneficial interests in its assets and the rights flowing from any
such beneficial interests. In paragraph 4 of the Initial Order, TLC was to “remain
in possession and control of their current and future assets, undertakings and
properties of every nature and kind whatsoever” (defined as the “Property”).
Pursuant to paras. 33 and 37 of that Order, the DIP Lenders’ Charge only
attached to and become “effective” as against the Property. While the
definition of “Property” subject to the charges granted in the Order, including
the DIP Lenders’ Charge, was further clarified as being those assets listed in
Schedule “B” to the Initial Order (which did reference the Binning House), that
reference did not have the effect of expanding the rights of the DIP Lenders
with respect to assets not beneficially owned by TLC.

[
310
]

Neither TLC nor the DIP Lenders made any submissions against the
proposition that they knew or had the means to easily discern that trust issues
were potentially arising in respect of many of TLC’s properties, including the
Binning House.

[
311
]

In these circumstances, the DIP Lenders are not in a position to
argue that they are
bona fide
lenders without notice, which was a
fundamental finding in
Gill
(para.
26
) and
Taylor Ventures
(BCSC,
paras. 35, 36). I do not mean to imply in any way that the DIP Lenders
acted inappropriately in this respect. Rather, they came into these proceedings
with their eyes open and made a calculated business decision to advance the DIP
funds even in light of the uncertainty regarding TLC’s ownership interests and the
consequent risks involved. Such is the lot of many DIP lenders but they take on
those risks given the substantial returns that they stand to gain through the
proceedings and their priority status under the court orders.

[
312
]

I also wish to return to certain fundamental propositions in
relation to TLC’s renewed arguments under this heading that the jurisdiction of
the court under
s. 11
of the
CCAA
allows the court to grant
“appropriate” relief so as allow this charitable property to be subject to the
payment of TLC’s creditors.

[
313
]

Consistent with the
BIA
provision quoted above, in
Heffner
v. Price Waterhouse Ltd.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 727 (BC CA)
, 10 B.C.L.R. (2d) 50 (C.A.), [1986] B.C.J. No. 1363,
the court upheld the fundamental principle that claims of creditors may only be
advanced against the interests of the bankrupt. In that case, even though the
bankrupt was the registered owner of certain real property, the
LTA
,
s. 23 statutory presumption did not prevent the true beneficial owners of
that property from asserting their claim against the trustee in bankruptcy.

[
314
]

As the AG argues, it would be anomalous indeed if a trustee could
unilaterally obtain beneficial interest in trust property comprising real
property simply by registered its interest under the
LTA
without any
notation as to the trust interests.

[
315
]

Although the
CCAA
does not include a
specific definition of “property”, the Act is replete with references to the “property”
of a “debtor company” or the “company”. In particular, and relevant to the DIP
Lenders’ position in this case, the
CCAA
provides:

Interim financing

11.2 (1)   On
application by a debtor company and on notice to the secured creditors who are
likely to be affected by the security or charge, a court may make an order
declaring that
all or part of the company’s property is subject to a
security or charge
— in an amount that the court considers appropriate — in
favour of a person specified in the order who agrees to lend to the company an
amount approved by the court as being required by the company, having regard to
its cash-flow statement. The security or charge may not secure an obligation
that exists before the order is made.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
316
]

As the court noted in
Century Services
, the
BIA
and
CCAA

share some commonalities: para. 22. In my view, another similarity is the
intention to allow creditors of the insolvent/bankrupt person to recover their
claims
only
with respect to the legal
and
beneficial interests of
that person.

[
317
]

The discretion afforded to the court under
s. 11
of the
CCAA

is a wide one, and as stated above, is intended to allow the court considerable
latitude in furthering the objectives of the
CCAA
towards avoiding the
social and economic losses arising from a failed or failing business. That
discretion is, however, not limitless (
Stelco Inc. (Re)
(2005),
2005 CanLII 8671 (ON CA)
, 75 O.R.
(3d) 5 (C.A.), [2005] O.J. No. 1171 at para.
44
); rather it must be
exercised on a principled basis and the appropriateness of the order relates to
not only the purpose of the order but also the means it employs:
Century
Services
at para. 70. Nevertheless, I am not aware of any case
authority by which that statutory jurisdiction under the
CCAA
has been
used to essentially expropriate the beneficial title of others for the benefit
of the restructuring proceedings.

[
318
]

Again, I have no doubt as to the
bona fides
of TLC in these
proceedings and its urgent need to restructure so that it can hopefully survive,
in some fashion, to continue making its positive and significant contributions
to conservancy. Many people involved in TLC have devoted countless volunteer hours
in the past and they continue to do so even today in furtherance of this worthy
cause and in these difficult circumstances.

[
319
]

However, I do not consider that the
CCAA
allows me to simply
disregard the property interests of others in furtherance of this cause.
Therefore, I reject TLC’s contention that even if it has no beneficial interest
in the Binning House because of the application of trust law and the
CPPA
,
it is within my jurisdiction, whether under the
LTA
,
CCAA
or
otherwise, to allow the DIP Lenders to seek payment from the sale of the
Binning House. This is so whether or not the Binning House has, at least notionally,
been made been subject to the DIP Lenders’ Charge under the Initial Order.

Conclusion

[
320
]

UBC’s application (its converted petition) for certain declaratory
relief in relation to its “fraud on powers” argument is dismissed, with costs payable
by UBC in favour of TLC.

[
321
]

TLC’s application for approval of the sale of the Binning House to
BJW/Mr. Wall is adjourned generally. TLC will have liberty to reset its
application with further evidence or it may file an amended application in
respect of any other relief that may be sought in respect of the Binning House.

“Fitzpatrick J.”
